lessons.plain: An operating system (OS) is the core software that runs a device: it manages the hardware, starts programs, stores files, and gives you a way to interact with the machine. Think of it as the manager of an apartment block. Tenants (apps) don't wire their own electricity; they ask the manager. Different OSes suit different jobs. Windows dominates office desktops. macOS runs Apple computers. Linux powers most servers. ChromeOS runs low-cost, browser-centred laptops. iOS and iPadOS run iPhones and iPads, and Android runs most other phones and tablets. Picking the right one means matching the device, the software people need, and the budget.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web hosting company needs to run hundreds of servers and does not want to pay a licence fee for each machine. Which kind of operating system would you guess they choose, and why?
lessons.teach:
An operating system (OS) is software that controls a device's hardware and provides services to the applications that run on it. The A+ exam expects you to match six common OSes to their purposes.

Windows, made by Microsoft, is the most common desktop and laptop OS in businesses. It runs the widest range of commercial software and games, and it can join centrally managed company networks. macOS, made by Apple, runs only on Apple's Mac computers and is popular for creative work. Linux is open source, meaning its code is publicly available and free to modify. It comes in distributions, which are packaged versions such as Ubuntu or Red Hat. Linux runs most web servers and many embedded devices, which are computers built into other equipment. ChromeOS, made by Google, is built on Linux but centred on the Chrome web browser. Chromebooks, the laptops that run it, are cheap and quick to start, and they keep most data in the cloud, meaning online services. iOS (for iPhone) and iPadOS (for iPad) are Apple's mobile OSes. Their apps come only through Apple's App Store, a download catalogue the vendor runs and checks. Android, made by Google, is built on the Linux kernel, the core part of an OS that talks to the hardware. It runs most non-Apple phones and tablets from many manufacturers and allows sideloading, which means installing apps from outside the official store.

This matters because each OS is tied to certain hardware, software catalogues and management tools. Choosing an OS therefore limits what users can run.

Worked example: a school wants 200 low-cost student laptops, used mostly for web-based assignments and managed centrally. Step 1: the main task is browser work. Step 2: the budget is tight. Step 3: the devices need central management and quick replacement. ChromeOS fits all three. Windows would also work but costs more per device, and macOS requires Apple hardware.

A common mistake is assuming ChromeOS or iPadOS can run any Windows desktop program. A specialist accounting application built for Windows will not install natively on them. If you roll those devices out without checking, staff cannot do their jobs. Always check software requirements before choosing the OS.

questions.prompt: A small hosting company is setting up 40 rack servers to run customer websites. It wants an OS whose code it can inspect and change without paying licence fees. Step 1: the main job is running web servers. Step 2: the company needs code that is publicly available and free to modify. Step 3: ______. Step 4: the company installs a Linux distribution (a packaged version of Linux), such as Ubuntu, on every server. Which statement correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Linux is open source and runs most web servers, so it meets both needs.
macOS is popular for creative work, so it suits servers that host design-heavy websites.
ChromeOS is built on Linux, so its browser-centred design makes it the best fit for web servers.
Windows is the most common OS in businesses, so it is the safest choice for any server role.
questions.why: Linux is the only option that is both open source (its code is free to view and modify) and the OS that runs most web servers, so it matches both requirements.

questions.prompt: A regional delivery firm gives its drivers phones from several manufacturers. The firm has built its own route app and wants to install it directly on the phones without publishing it in any official store. Which mobile OS supports this?
choices: Android, because it allows sideloading, which means installing apps from outside the official store
iOS, because Apple checks every app in its App Store before drivers install it
iPadOS, because tablets can install apps from any source
ChromeOS, because it keeps most data in online services
questions.why: Android runs on phones from many manufacturers and allows sideloading, while iOS and iPadOS apps come only through Apple's App Store.

questions.prompt: In the description of Android, what is the kernel?
choices: The official download catalogue that the vendor runs and checks
The core part of an OS that talks to the hardware
A packaged version of Linux, such as Ubuntu or Red Hat
A computer built into another piece of equipment
questions.why: The kernel is the core of an OS that communicates with the hardware; Android is built on the Linux kernel.

questions.prompt: A law office buys 15 iPads for its paralegals, planning to use them for a case-management program that was built only for Windows desktops. Nobody checked the software requirements first. What is the most likely result?
choices: The program installs from the App Store once the iPads join the company network
The program runs normally because iPadOS can run any desktop program
The program runs only after the iPads are rebooted into a Linux distribution
The program will not install natively, so the paralegals cannot do that part of their work
questions.why: iPadOS cannot natively run Windows desktop programs, so choosing the device without checking software requirements leaves staff unable to work.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between Windows, macOS, Linux, ChromeOS, iOS/iPadOS and Android for a new set of devices. Name at least one limit or tradeoff of a cheaper or more locked-down option.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with what people actually need to run, then look at hardware and budget. Windows is the safe default for office desktops because it runs the most business software and fits company-managed networks. macOS only comes on Apple hardware, so it costs more, but creative teams often prefer it. Linux is free and open source and comes in distributions, so it is the usual choice for servers. ChromeOS is cheap and easy to manage because it is browser-centred, but the tradeoff is that it can't natively run many Windows desktop programs. On phones and tablets, iOS and iPadOS only install apps from Apple's App Store, which is safer but less flexible. Android comes from many manufacturers and allows sideloading, which gives more flexibility but more risk. So I check software requirements first, before cost.
rubricPoints: Defines an OS as software that manages hardware and runs applications.
Matches Windows to business desktops and broad software support.
Matches Linux to servers and notes it is open source with distributions.
Describes ChromeOS as low-cost and browser-centred, with limited native desktop software.
Distinguishes iOS/iPadOS's single app store from Android's multi-vendor, sideload-capable model.
Names a tradeoff, such as cost versus software compatibility or control versus flexibility.

suggested.rationale: This objective is tested through short scenarios where you must pick the right OS for a user's needs, so reasoning through exam-style situations helps more than any hands-on mission.

lessons.plain: Windows ships with a set of built-in toolboxes for looking at and changing what the computer is doing. Task Manager shows what is running right now and lets you stop a frozen program. Disk Management shows your drives and lets you prepare or resize them. Control Panel and the Settings app are the two places where everyday options live, old style and new style. MMC is an empty frame that holds specialist tools called snap-ins. Think of a mechanic's garage: you reach for the right wrench instead of trying every drawer.
lessons.guessPrompt: A program has frozen and will not close when you click its X button. Which built-in Windows tool would you open to force it closed, and roughly what would you click?
lessons.teach:
Windows administrative tools are the built-in programs for viewing and changing system state. Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc) lists processes, meaning programs currently running, with their CPU, memory, disk and network use. It also has a Startup tab for apps that launch at sign-in and a Services tab. Disk Management (diskmgmt.msc) shows physical disks and partitions, which are separate sections of a disk. With it you can initialize a new disk, create, extend, shrink or format a volume (a usable formatted area), and assign a drive letter. Control Panel is the older settings hub, with Programs and Features, power options and user accounts. The Settings app is the newer hub that Microsoft is moving options into, so many settings appear in both places. MMC, the Microsoft Management Console, is a frame that hosts snap-ins, which are plug-in admin tools. Examples are Device Manager (hardware and drivers), Event Viewer (system logs), Services (background programs and their startup type), Local Users and Groups, Task Scheduler, Certificate Manager, and Group Policy Editor (gpedit.msc, which holds rules applied to the machine). Computer Management bundles several snap-ins in one window. These tools work because each one reads and writes the same underlying configuration, and each is built for one job. Choosing the right one is faster and safer than hunting.

Worked example: a user says the PC is slow and a new second drive is missing. Step 1: open Task Manager, go to Processes, and sort by CPU. One unresponsive app is at 95 percent, so choose End task. Step 2: on the Startup tab, disable that app so it does not launch at sign-in. Step 3: the drive is not in File Explorer, so open Disk Management. Disk 1 shows Not Initialized. Initialize it, create a new simple volume, format it NTFS, and assign the letter E. Step 4: check Event Viewer for disk errors to confirm the hardware is healthy.

Common mistake: right-clicking the wrong disk in Disk Management and deleting or formatting a volume. That erases its data at once, and on a running server it breaks anything that relied on that drive. Check the disk number, size and label before any change. Also, ending a process only stops it for now. If a service keeps restarting it, change its startup type in Services.

questions.prompt: At a small veterinary clinic, the front-desk PC is sluggish. A technician works through it as follows. Step 1: open Task Manager with Ctrl+Shift+Esc, go to Processes, and sort by memory. A program called PetSyncAgent is using 3 GB, so the technician selects it and chooses End task. Step 2: two minutes later, PetSyncAgent is back in the list, using memory again. The technician learns that a background service relaunches it every time it stops. Step 3: ______. Step 4: restart the PC and open Task Manager again to confirm that PetSyncAgent no longer appears. What belongs in Step 3?
choices: Open the Services snap-in, find the service behind PetSyncAgent, and change its startup type so it no longer starts automatically
Open Device Manager and uninstall the driver for the PC's network adapter
Choose End task on PetSyncAgent again each time it reappears, until it stops returning
Open Disk Management and format the volume where PetSyncAgent is installed
questions.why: Ending a process only stops it for now, so when a service keeps restarting it, the lasting fix is to change that service's startup type in Services.

questions.prompt: In Windows, what is an MMC snap-in?
choices: A program that Task Manager lists on its Startup tab because it launches at sign-in
A partition on a disk that has been formatted and given a drive letter
A plug-in admin tool, such as Device Manager or Event Viewer, that runs inside the Microsoft Management Console frame
An older settings hub that holds Programs and Features, power options and user accounts
questions.why: MMC is a frame that hosts snap-ins, which are plug-in admin tools such as Device Manager, Event Viewer and Services.

questions.prompt: At an accounting firm, a newly connected label printer does not work. The technician suspects that its driver (the software that lets Windows talk to the hardware) is missing or faulty. Which built-in tool is built for checking hardware and its drivers?
choices: Disk Management
Task Scheduler
Device Manager
Local Users and Groups
questions.why: Device Manager is the snap-in for viewing hardware and managing its drivers.

questions.prompt: On a running file server, a technician plans to shrink a volume on a disk labelled Archive in Disk Management. Two disks in the list are both 800 GB. What should the technician do before making the change, and why?
choices: Initialize both disks first, because Disk Management cannot shrink a volume on a disk that is already initialized
End every process in Task Manager, because Disk Management will not open while programs are running
Open the Settings app instead, because Disk Management can only create volumes and cannot change existing ones
Confirm the disk number, size and label match the intended disk, because changing the wrong volume can erase data and break services that rely on it
questions.why: Acting on the wrong disk can destroy data at once and break anything that depends on that drive, so the disk number, size and label must be checked before any change.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between Task Manager, Disk Management, Control Panel or Settings, and an MMC snap-in for a given problem. Name one limit or risk of at least one of these tools.
lessons.modelAnswer: I match the tool to the kind of problem. If something is running badly right now, like a frozen app or high CPU, I open Task Manager. It shows live processes, lets me end one, and lets me stop apps from launching at sign-in. If the problem is storage, such as a new drive that isn't showing up or a volume that needs resizing, I use Disk Management to initialize, partition, format or assign letters. For everyday options like display, apps or power, I use Settings or Control Panel, since many options live in both. For deeper admin work I use MMC snap-ins: Device Manager for drivers, Event Viewer for logs, Services for startup types, and Group Policy Editor for machine rules. The main risk is Disk Management, because deleting or formatting the wrong volume wipes its data instantly. Another limit is that ending a process in Task Manager is temporary if a service restarts it.
rubricPoints: Task Manager is for live processes, resource use and startup apps.
Disk Management is for initializing, partitioning, formatting and lettering disks.
Control Panel is the legacy settings hub and the Settings app is its modern replacement, with overlap between them.
MMC is a container that hosts snap-ins such as Device Manager, Event Viewer and Services.
The explanation names a real risk or limit, such as data loss from the wrong Disk Management action or ending a process being only temporary.

suggested.rationale: No current mission runs on Windows, and the core exam skill is choosing the right native tool for a described symptom, which scenario-based reasoning practises best.

lessons.plain: The Windows command line is a text window where you type instructions instead of clicking through menus. Windows has two: Command Prompt (cmd), the older shell, and PowerShell, a newer shell whose commands return structured data you can filter and pass along. Think of it like ordering at a counter by naming exactly what you want instead of wandering the aisles. It is faster, it works on machines with no usable desktop, and it lets you repeat the same fix on many computers. For a technician, knowing a handful of commands means you can check network settings, repair system files, manage disks and users quickly.
lessons.guessPrompt: A user says a website will not load, but their chat app still works. If you could type only one or two short commands to see whether the computer can find that website's address on the network, what would you want those commands to check?
lessons.teach:
A shell is a program that reads typed commands and runs them. Command Prompt (cmd.exe) runs classic commands; PowerShell runs those plus cmdlets, verb-noun commands such as Get-Process (list running programs) or Get-Service (list background services). Cmdlets output objects, data with named fields, so one command's output can be piped (sent with the | symbol) into another, as in Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU. Adding /? after a cmd command, or using Get-Help in PowerShell, shows its options.

Common groups to know. Files and folders: cd (change directory), dir (list contents), md and rmdir (make and remove a folder), copy, xcopy and robocopy (robust copy that can retry and mirror folders). Networking: ipconfig (show address settings; /release, /renew, /flushdns), ping (test reachability), tracert (show each hop on the path), nslookup (ask DNS, the name-to-address service), netstat (list active connections), hostname. System health: sfc /scannow (System File Checker, repairs protected Windows files), chkdsk (checks a disk for file system errors), winver (shows the Windows version). Disks: diskpart and format. Accounts and policy: net user, net use (map a network share to a drive letter), whoami, gpupdate /force (reapply Group Policy, the central settings pushed by a domain) and gpresult /r (show which policies applied). Power: shutdown /r /t 0 restarts now.

Worked example: a site will not load. Run ipconfig: the PC has a normal address and gateway. Run ping 8.8.8.8: replies arrive, so the internet path works. Run nslookup example.com: it fails, so name lookup is the problem. Run ipconfig /flushdns to clear stale cached names, then retry.

Common mistake: running sfc, chkdsk repairs or diskpart in a normal window. These need an elevated (Run as administrator) prompt and will refuse or fail otherwise. Worse, diskpart and format act immediately; selecting the wrong disk erases real data on a running system, so always list and confirm the target first.

questions.prompt: At a small accounting firm, IT published a new Group Policy (central settings pushed by the domain) that maps a shared folder to drive S:. One laptop still has no S: drive. The technician works through it like this. Step 1: run whoami, which confirms the user is signed in with the correct domain account. Step 2: run gpresult /r, which shows the new policy is not in the list of applied policies. Step 3: ??? Step 4: run gpresult /r again, which now lists the new policy, then have the user sign out and back in so the drive mapping appears. Which command belongs in Step 3?
choices: net user, to list the local accounts on the laptop
ipconfig /flushdns, to clear stale cached names so the share can be found
gpupdate /force, to make the laptop reapply Group Policy now
sfc /scannow, to repair protected Windows files that may block policy
questions.why: gpresult /r showed the policy had not applied yet, and gpupdate /force tells the PC to reapply Group Policy right away, which the second gpresult /r then confirms.

questions.prompt: A technician at a print shop runs Get-Service | Sort-Object Status in PowerShell and gets a neatly ordered list of services. Why does piping one cmdlet into another work this way?
choices: Sort-Object reads the screen text and guesses where each column begins
Cmdlets output objects with named fields, so the next command can sort on a field such as Status
Get-Service saves its results to a file that Sort-Object opens afterward
The | symbol launches cmd.exe, which does the sorting for PowerShell
questions.why: PowerShell cmdlets pass objects, data with named fields, through the pipe, so Sort-Object can sort directly on the Status field.

questions.prompt: Staff at a branch office can reach some company servers, but a file server at head office times out. The technician wants to see each router hop along the path to find where traffic stops. Which command fits best?
choices: netstat
hostname
nslookup
tracert
questions.why: tracert shows each hop on the path to a destination, so the technician can see the point where replies stop coming back.

questions.prompt: A school technician needs to wipe a USB stick with diskpart on a PC that also has two internal drives holding student records. What should the technician do before selecting a disk?
choices: Run format on the drive letter first, because format asks for confirmation
Run diskpart in a normal window so it cannot change anything by accident
Select disk 0, because the removable drive is normally listed first
Open an elevated prompt, list the disks and confirm which one is the USB stick, for example by its size
questions.why: diskpart needs an elevated prompt and acts immediately, so listing and confirming the target disk first prevents erasing the wrong drive's real data.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would reach for Command Prompt versus PowerShell for a support task, give one example of each, and name one risk or limit of working from the command line.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both are text shells for running Windows commands. Command Prompt is fine for quick classic tools: ipconfig to check an address, ping and nslookup to see whether a problem is reachability or DNS, sfc /scannow to repair system files. PowerShell runs those too, but its cmdlets, like Get-Service or Get-Process, return objects with named fields, so I can pipe them into Sort-Object or Where-Object and filter results, or script the same change across many PCs. The tradeoff is power versus safety. Commands run instantly with no undo screen, so diskpart or format on the wrong disk wipes data, and many repair tools need an elevated administrator prompt, which means a mistake has system-wide reach. I list and confirm targets before destructive commands, and I check options with /? or Get-Help.
rubricPoints: Defines a shell and distinguishes Command Prompt from PowerShell cmdlets that output objects.
Gives a correct example command matched to a realistic task.
Mentions piping or filtering as a PowerShell advantage.
Notes that some tools require an elevated administrator prompt.
Names a real risk such as destructive disk commands acting immediately with no undo.

suggested.rationale: No current mission uses Windows shells, and the exam tests choosing the right command for a described symptom, so reasoning through scenario questions builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Windows computers on the same network can be organized in two ways. In a workgroup, every PC is its own boss: it keeps its own list of users and passwords, like separate houses each with its own key. In a domain, a central server holds one list of users and rules for every PC, like an office building where one security desk issues badges that open the right doors anywhere. On top of either arrangement, a PC can share a folder or a printer so other people on the network can use it, and the computer decides who gets in and what they may do.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small office has five Windows PCs, and each PC keeps its own separate list of user accounts. An employee changes her password on PC 1. What do you expect happens when she logs on to PC 2 with the new password, and why?
lessons.teach:
A workgroup is a peer-to-peer arrangement where each Windows PC stores its own local accounts. Nothing is shared centrally, so a password change on one PC does not reach the others. Workgroups suit roughly ten or fewer machines. A domain is a centrally managed group of computers. A server called a domain controller runs Active Directory, a directory service that stores every user, group and computer account and pushes settings through Group Policy (centrally applied rules). Users log on to any joined PC with one account. Joining a domain requires a Pro, Enterprise or Education edition, because Home editions cannot join. You join through System Properties or Settings by entering the domain name and an admin credential, then you restart.

A network share is a folder made available to other computers. It is reached by a UNC path such as \\SERVER\Sales, which means two backslashes, the computer name, then the share name. Two permission layers apply. Share permissions control network access only. NTFS permissions are file-system rules that apply both locally and over the network. Over the network, the more restrictive of the two wins.

Here is a worked example. The share permission is Everyone: Read, and the NTFS permission is Sales group: Modify. First, Ana in Sales opens \\SERVER\Sales from her laptop. Second, the share layer allows only Read. Third, the NTFS layer allows Modify. Fourth, the stricter result is Read, so she cannot save. If she sat at the server itself, only NTFS would apply and she could edit.

Printer sharing works the same way. You enable sharing in the printer's properties, and clients connect using \\PCNAME\PrinterShare, with drivers supplied by the host.

A common mistake is leaving the network profile set to Public. The Public profile turns off network discovery and file and printer sharing, so shares look broken even though they are configured correctly. On a trusted LAN, use the Private profile. On a domain, the Domain profile is used.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm shares a folder on its file server, FS02, as Payroll. The share permission is Everyone: Full Control. The NTFS permission is Accounting group: Read. Ben, who is in Accounting, opens \\FS02\Payroll from his desktop and tries to save an edited spreadsheet. Step 1: Ben connects over the network, so both permission layers apply. Step 2: The share layer allows Full Control. Step 3: ??? Step 4: The stricter of the two results is Read, so Ben can open the file but cannot save changes. Which statement correctly fills in Step 3?
choices: The NTFS layer is skipped, because NTFS only applies to someone sitting at the server.
The NTFS layer allows Accounting only Read.
The two layers are added together, so Ben gets Full Control plus Read.
Share Full Control overrides NTFS, because the share layer is checked first.
questions.why: Over the network both layers apply and the more restrictive one wins, so Step 3 has to be the NTFS layer granting only Read, which then beats the share layer's Full Control.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has 45 staff who move between desks. Management wants each person to sign in to any office PC with a single account and wants security rules applied to every machine from one place. Which setup meets these needs?
choices: A workgroup, with the same local account created by hand on every PC.
A workgroup, with every PC's network profile set to Private.
A network share at \\HR\Accounts that holds everyone's password.
A domain, with a domain controller running Active Directory and pushing Group Policy.
questions.why: Only a domain gives one account that works on any joined PC, plus centrally applied rules through Group Policy. A workgroup keeps separate local accounts on each PC and suits about ten or fewer machines.

questions.prompt: At a veterinary clinic, a technician has set up a share and its permissions correctly on the reception PC. On the clinic's trusted office network, other PCs still cannot find the share or the shared label printer. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The share's NTFS permission is more restrictive than its share permission.
The reception PC's network profile is set to Public.
The UNC path must start with one backslash instead of two.
The clinic's PCs are in a workgroup rather than a domain.
questions.why: The Public profile turns off network discovery and file and printer sharing, so correctly configured shares look broken. On a trusted LAN the Private profile should be used.

questions.prompt: A new hire at an architecture firm brings a laptop running Windows 11 Home. IT enters the firm's domain name and an admin credential in System Properties, but the laptop cannot join the domain. What must change before it can join?
choices: Upgrade the laptop to a Pro, Enterprise or Education edition.
Switch the laptop's network profile from Private to Domain before joining.
Share a folder on the laptop so the domain controller can reach it.
Create a local account on the laptop that matches the user's domain account.
questions.why: Home editions cannot join a domain. The laptop needs a Pro, Enterprise or Education edition, and after joining it must be restarted.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a growing office might move from a workgroup to a domain, how share and NTFS permissions combine when someone opens a shared folder, and name one cost or limit of choosing a domain.
lessons.modelAnswer: In a workgroup, every PC keeps its own accounts. That is fine for a handful of machines, but each password change or new hire has to be repeated on every PC. A domain puts all accounts in Active Directory on a domain controller. People sign in anywhere with one account, and admins push settings with Group Policy. The cost is that you need a server to buy and maintain, and if the domain controller is down, logons and policy suffer. Every PC also needs a Pro-class edition, because Home cannot join a domain. For shared folders, network users pass through two gates. Share permissions apply only over the network, while NTFS permissions apply everywhere. The stricter result wins, so Share Read plus NTFS Modify means Read over the network. Also check that the network profile is Private or Domain, not Public, or discovery and sharing stay off.
rubricPoints: A workgroup stores accounts locally on each PC, while a domain centralizes them on a domain controller running Active Directory.
Home editions cannot join a domain.
Shares are reached by a UNC path of the form \\computer\share.
Over the network, the more restrictive of share and NTFS permissions applies, while locally only NTFS applies.
The Public network profile disables discovery and file and printer sharing.
A domain adds cost and a central dependency on the domain controller.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine covers Windows sharing, and exam questions present scenarios like an access-denied share or a PC that will not join a domain, so reasoning through exam-style situations adds the most.

lessons.plain: Windows comes in several editions, which are versions of the same operating system with different feature sets and prices. Home suits personal use. Pro adds tools that businesses need, and Enterprise and Education add more for large organizations. Installing Windows can be done two ways. An in-place upgrade installs the new version on top of the old one and keeps your files, apps and settings. A clean install wipes the drive and starts fresh. Think of moving house: an in-place upgrade is renovating while you live there, and a clean install is demolishing and rebuilding on an empty lot.
lessons.guessPrompt: A user's laptop is slow and keeps crashing because years of leftover junk and a possible infection have built up. Would you install the new Windows version on top of the old one, or wipe the drive and start fresh? Why?
lessons.teach:
A Windows edition is a feature tier of the same operating system. Home covers personal basics. It cannot join a domain, which is a centrally managed group of computers run by a server called a domain controller. It lacks BitLocker, which is full-drive encryption, and the Group Policy editor, a tool for enforcing settings. It also cannot act as a Remote Desktop host, meaning other people cannot connect into it remotely. Pro adds all of these and supports far more RAM. Enterprise, sold through volume licensing (bulk agreements for organizations), adds advanced security and management features. Education is similar to Enterprise and is priced for schools. Windows 11 also requires UEFI firmware (the modern replacement for BIOS), Secure Boot, and TPM 2.0, a security chip that stores encryption keys.

An in-place upgrade runs setup from inside the running OS and keeps files, apps and settings. It is fast and causes little disruption, but it carries existing problems forward. A clean install boots from installation media such as a USB stick or a network boot. It repartitions or formats the drive, which erases it, and then installs fresh. That removes corruption and malware, but you must back up data and reinstall the apps afterward.

Worked example: a five-person office runs Windows Home and is adding a domain controller. First, Home cannot join a domain, so the edition must change. Second, an edition upgrade from Home to Pro only needs a Pro product key entered in Settings, and it keeps all data. Third, after the upgrade, join each PC to the domain. No wipe is needed.

Common mistake: you cannot in-place upgrade from 32-bit to 64-bit Windows, and you cannot downgrade editions this way. Both require a clean install. Another mistake is starting a clean install without a verified backup, which permanently loses user data. Choose in-place when the system is healthy and continuity matters, and choose clean when the system is unstable, compromised, or changing architecture.

questions.prompt: A small design studio has one workstation running 32-bit Windows 10 Pro. It keeps crashing, a malware scan found infections, and the owner needs 64-bit Windows so a new rendering app will run. The technician's plan: Step 1: Recognise that moving from 32-bit to 64-bit cannot be done as an in-place upgrade, and the system is also unstable and compromised, so a clean install is the right choice. Step 2: ???. Step 3: Boot the workstation from a 64-bit Windows USB installer, repartition and format the drive, and install fresh. Step 4: Reinstall the studio's apps and copy the user files back. Which action belongs in Step 2?
choices: Enter a 64-bit product key in Settings so the 32-bit system converts itself without a wipe
Copy the user files to an external drive and confirm the copy opens before touching the internal drive
Skip the backup, because a clean install from USB leaves the user's files in place on the drive
Run 64-bit setup from inside the running 32-bit Windows so the apps and settings carry over
questions.why: A clean install formats and erases the drive, so a verified backup must be made first or the studio's files are lost for good.

questions.prompt: A freelance accountant works alone from home. She wants full-drive encryption on her laptop in case it is stolen, and she wants her bookkeeper to be able to connect into the laptop remotely using Remote Desktop. She does not have a volume licensing agreement. What is the lowest Windows edition that meets both needs?
choices: Home, because it covers personal users and includes encryption
Enterprise, because BitLocker is sold only through volume licensing
Pro, because it adds BitLocker and can act as a Remote Desktop host
Education, because it is the cheapest tier that includes BitLocker
questions.why: Home lacks BitLocker and cannot be a Remote Desktop host, while Pro adds both without needing the volume licensing that Enterprise requires.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic has a laptop running Windows 10 Pro. It is stable, has no known malware, and has UEFI firmware, Secure Boot and TPM 2.0. The receptionist relies on many installed apps and saved settings, and the clinic wants as little downtime as possible when moving to Windows 11. Which approach fits best?
choices: An in-place upgrade run from inside Windows, keeping the files, apps and settings
A clean install from USB, because every Windows 11 move must format the drive
A clean install over a network boot, because it keeps the apps while erasing old files
An edition downgrade to Home first, then a clean install to reach Windows 11
questions.why: The system is healthy, meets the Windows 11 hardware requirements and continuity matters, which is exactly when an in-place upgrade is the right choice.

questions.prompt: A charity received ten donated PCs that run Windows Enterprise. Its licences only cover Windows Pro, so a volunteer plans to run setup from inside each PC to switch it to Pro while keeping all the files and apps. What will happen with this plan?
choices: It will not work, because moving down an edition cannot be done in place and needs a clean install
It will not work, because Pro cannot run on hardware that has TPM 2.0
It will work, but only if the PCs are first joined to a domain controller
It will work, because entering a Pro product key in Settings changes any edition while keeping data
questions.why: Downgrading editions is not possible as an in-place upgrade, so the PCs need a backup and a clean install of Pro.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between an in-place upgrade and a clean install, and how the Windows edition affects that decision. Name at least one limit or tradeoff of each approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I check the edition against what the business needs. Home cannot join a domain, use BitLocker, use the Group Policy editor, or host Remote Desktop. If the business needs any of those, the machine needs Pro or higher. Moving from Home to Pro is just a key change and keeps the user's data. Next I pick the install type. An in-place upgrade keeps files, apps and settings, so it is quick and easy on the user. The tradeoff is that it carries over any corruption or malware already on the system. A clean install wipes the drive and gives a known-good system. Its cost is time: I must back up data first and reinstall the apps afterward. Some changes force a clean install, such as moving from 32-bit to 64-bit or downgrading to a lower edition.
rubricPoints: Names features Home lacks that Pro provides, such as domain join, BitLocker, Group Policy editor, or Remote Desktop host.
States that an in-place upgrade keeps files, apps and settings but carries existing problems forward.
States that a clean install wipes the drive, giving a fresh system but requiring a backup and app reinstall.
Identifies a case that forces a clean install, such as a 32-bit to 64-bit change or an edition downgrade.
Recommends verifying a backup before any install that erases data.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly about choosing the right edition and install method for a given situation, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios builds the skill better than any existing mission or engine.

lessons.plain: Windows keeps itself healthy with three separate safety habits. Windows Update downloads fixes and new features from Microsoft. Backup copies your personal files somewhere else, such as an external drive, so you can get them back if they are deleted or the disk dies. System Restore takes snapshots of the computer's settings and system files so you can rewind the system to an earlier, working state without touching your documents. Think of a house: updates are repairs, backup is a copy of your belongings stored at a friend's place, and System Restore is undoing a bad renovation while leaving your furniture where it is.
lessons.guessPrompt: A user installs a new graphics driver and the PC starts crashing. They also have an important spreadsheet they deleted last week. Do you think one Windows recovery tool can fix both problems, or would you need two different tools? Why?
lessons.teach:
Windows Update is the built-in service that installs patches. Quality updates are monthly security and bug fixes. Feature updates are larger version upgrades. In the Settings app you can view update history, pause updates for a while, and uninstall a recent update that caused trouble. When updates fail, the usual checks are: restart to finish any pending install, confirm there is enough free disk space, run the built-in Windows Update troubleshooter, and read the error code shown in update history.

System Restore rolls back system files, the registry (the central settings database), installed programs and drivers to an earlier restore point. A restore point is a saved snapshot, created automatically before updates or driver installs, or manually by you. It works because Windows records those system pieces before a change, so it can put them back. It does not save or restore personal files.

Backup protects user data. File History regularly copies files from your libraries and desktop to another drive, keeping older versions. Backup and Restore (Windows 7), still present in newer Windows, can also make a system image, which is a full copy of the whole drive for rebuilding after a disk failure.

Worked example: a driver update causes crashes. First, start in Safe Mode, a minimal startup that loads only basic drivers. Second, open System Restore and pick the point created just before the driver install. Third, confirm and reboot. The old driver returns and the crashes stop. Fourth, the deleted spreadsheet still has to come from File History, because System Restore never held it.

Common mistake: treating System Restore as a backup. If the disk fails or a file is deleted, restore points will not help, and System Restore is often turned off by default on some systems. On a running system, that mistake means permanent data loss. Real protection needs updates, restore points and separate file backups working together.

questions.prompt:
At a small accounting firm, a laptop installed a monthly quality update (a security and bug-fix patch) overnight. Now its scanning software crashes every time it opens. The technician works through it:
Step 1: Open the Settings app, view the update history, and confirm that exactly one quality update was installed last night.
Step 2: ____
Step 3: Pause updates for a while so the same update is not reinstalled before the scanner vendor releases a fix.
Step 4: Open the scanning software again. It now launches normally.
Which action is the missing Step 2?
choices: Run System Restore so it brings back the scanned documents saved since last night
Use File History to bring back an older version of the scanning program's files
Uninstall that recent quality update from the update history in Settings
Create a system image with Backup and Restore (Windows 7) and then reboot the laptop
questions.why: The Settings app can uninstall a recent update that caused trouble, which removes the change that broke the scanner before Step 3 pauses updates.

questions.prompt: A graphic design studio wants to protect one workstation against a dead disk. If the disk fails, they want to rebuild the entire drive onto a new disk: the operating system, the programs and the files. Which tool fits that goal?
choices: Running the built-in Windows Update troubleshooter once every month
A system image made with Backup and Restore (Windows 7)
A manual System Restore point created before the next driver installation
Pausing feature updates so the workstation's version stays the same
questions.why: A system image is a full copy of the whole drive, made for rebuilding after a disk failure. Restore points, update settings and troubleshooters do not copy the drive.

questions.prompt: On a public library kiosk PC, the same quality update has failed to install three times. The technician has already restarted the PC to finish any pending install. The disk shows only 1 GB of free space. What is the most sensible next step?
choices: Run System Restore so it deletes the failed update and lets the install retry
Skip this patch and install the next feature update to replace it
Turn on File History so it keeps copies of the update's installation files
Free up disk space, then try installing the update again
questions.why: Too little free disk space is a common cause of failed updates. Since the restart is already done, making room for the update is the logical next check.

questions.prompt: Two days ago, a user at a veterinary clinic deleted a folder of 40 invoices. A colleague suggests running System Restore to a restore point made three days ago, before the deletion. What will happen to the invoices?
choices: They stay deleted, because System Restore does not save or restore personal files
They come back, but every program installed since the restore point is removed
Nothing can run, because restore points are only created for feature updates
They come back, because the restore point was made before the folder was deleted
questions.why: System Restore rolls back system files, the registry, programs and drivers only. Deleted personal files must come from a separate file backup such as File History.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between System Restore and a file backup like File History, and say when you would use each. Include one thing System Restore cannot do.
lessons.modelAnswer: System Restore and File History solve different problems. System Restore rewinds the operating system itself: system files, the registry, drivers and installed programs, back to a restore point, which is a snapshot Windows usually takes before updates or installs. I would use it when a bad driver or update makes the PC unstable, often starting in Safe Mode first. Its limit is that it does not protect personal files. If a user deletes a document or the drive fails, System Restore cannot bring the data back, and restore points live on the same disk. File History copies user files to another drive and keeps older versions, so I would use it to recover deleted or overwritten documents. For a dead disk, a full system image is better. The tradeoff is that backups need extra storage and someone to check they actually run.
rubricPoints: System Restore rolls back system files, registry, drivers and programs to a restore point.
System Restore does not back up or recover personal files.
File History copies personal files to a separate drive and keeps versions.
A system image is needed to rebuild after a full disk failure.
A bad update can also be uninstalled from Windows Update history.
Backups cost storage and must be checked to be trustworthy.

suggested.rationale: No current mission covers Windows recovery, and the exam tests choosing the right tool for a described failure, so reasoning through scenarios builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: macOS (Apple's desktop system) and Linux (a free system used on most servers) are both Unix-like. That means they work alike under the hood. Neither uses drive letters such as C:. Instead, everything hangs off one folder tree that starts at a single top folder called root. Both also share many short typed commands for moving around, managing files, and checking the system. Think of two cars from different makers with the same pedal layout: once you can drive one, the other feels familiar. This lesson covers the built-in features, disk formats, habits, and commands a technician uses on each.
lessons.guessPrompt: On a Linux server you can't see in a window, how might you find out which disk or folder is almost full, using only typed commands?
lessons.teach:
macOS and Linux are Unix-like operating systems. Both use one directory tree starting at the root, written /, rather than drive letters. A terminal is a text window where you type commands to a shell, the program that runs them.

These are the macOS features to know. Finder is the file browser. Spotlight is system-wide search. Keychain is a stored-password vault. FileVault is full-disk encryption. Time Machine makes automatic incremental backups to an external drive. Mission Control shows all open windows and desktops. A file system is the format that organises data on a disk. macOS defaults to APFS (Apple File System). Linux usually uses ext4 or XFS. Both systems read FAT32 and exFAT for removable drives.

These are the core commands. pwd shows your current folder. ls lists files. cd changes folder. cp copies. mv moves or renames. rm deletes with no recycle bin. cat prints a file. nano is a simple editor. grep searches text for a pattern. find locates files. df shows free space per file system. du shows how much space a folder uses. ps and top list running processes, and kill stops one by its process ID. chmod changes permissions, meaning who may read, write, or run a file. chown changes the owner. ip addr shows network settings. man opens a command's manual. sudo runs one command with administrator (root) rights, and su switches user. apt (Ubuntu/Debian) and dnf (Fedora/Red Hat) are package managers, tools that install and update software.

Here is a worked example for a full Linux server. First, run df -h (-h means human-readable sizes); / shows 98% used. Next, run sudo du -sh /var/* to total each folder; /var/log holds 30 GB. Then run ls -lh /var/log and spot one huge old log. Finally, confirm it is not needed, then compress or remove it.

A common mistake is putting sudo in front of everything, or working as root. One mistyped rm can then wipe system files with no undo. Best practice is to use a normal account and sudo only when needed. Keep the system patched through the package manager or macOS Software Update, and back up regularly.

questions.prompt: At a small accounting firm, the fan on an Ubuntu Linux desktop is roaring and the machine is sluggish. Here is how a technician fixes it. Step 1: open a terminal and run top, which lists running processes; a process named reportgen is using 99% of the CPU, and its process ID is 5307. Step 2: ask the user, who confirms it is a stuck report job that is safe to stop. Step 3: ______. Step 4: run top again; CPU use is back to normal and the fan quiets down. Which action belongs in Step 3?
choices: Run chmod on reportgen to take away its CPU access
Run rm 5307 to delete the running process
Run df -h to free up CPU time used by reportgen
Run kill 5307 to stop the process by its process ID
questions.why: kill stops a running process when you give it the process ID that top or ps showed, whereas rm deletes files, df shows disk space, and chmod changes file permissions.

questions.prompt: A law office wants every MacBook protected so that if a laptop is stolen, nobody can read the data on its disk. Which macOS feature does this?
choices: Keychain
Spotlight
FileVault
Time Machine
questions.why: FileVault is macOS full-disk encryption; Keychain stores passwords, Time Machine makes backups, and Spotlight is search.

questions.prompt: A designer at a print shop needs one USB flash drive that can be read on both a Mac and a Linux laptop. Which file system should the drive be formatted with?
choices: APFS
XFS
ext4
exFAT
questions.why: Both macOS and Linux read exFAT on removable drives, while APFS is the macOS default and ext4 and XFS are typical Linux disk formats.

questions.prompt: At a veterinary clinic, a technician logs in to a Linux server as root all day for convenience. One afternoon a mistyped rm command deletes system files. What best practice would have reduced this risk?
choices: Use su to switch to root, since su is safer than logging in directly as root
Work in a normal account and use sudo only for commands that need admin rights
Stay as root but restore the deleted files from the recycle bin afterwards
Run every command with sudo so each one is checked before it runs
questions.why: rm has no recycle bin, so working as a normal user and adding sudo only when needed limits how much damage one typo can do.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who only knows Windows how you would check disk space and fix a full disk on a Linux machine, and name one risk or tradeoff of using sudo to do it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Linux has no C: drive. Everything sits under one tree starting at /. I'd run df -h to see how full each file system is in readable sizes. If / is nearly full, I'd run du -sh on folders such as /var/* to see which one is big. Then I'd use ls -lh to find the specific large files, often old logs. Reading system folders may need sudo, which runs one command with root (administrator) rights. The tradeoff is that sudo removes the safety net. rm has no recycle bin, so a typo under sudo can delete system files permanently. I'd confirm a file isn't needed and prefer compressing it over deleting. I'd also stay on a normal account and use sudo only for the specific command that needs it.
rubricPoints: States that Linux and macOS use one directory tree from / instead of drive letters.
Uses df to see free space per file system and du to find large folders.
Defines sudo as running a single command with root or administrator rights.
Names the risk that rm under sudo deletes permanently with no recycle bin.
Recommends least privilege: a normal account and sudo only when needed.

suggested.rationale: Moving around a real server with pwd, ls, cd, and related commands builds the command fluency this objective tests better than reading a list.

lessons.plain: Physical security controls are the things that stop someone from simply walking up to a computer, a server room, or a laptop and touching it. Passwords and encryption protect data once someone is at the keyboard. Physical controls decide who gets to the keyboard at all. Think of a hotel. A key card opens only your floor and room. A front desk checks faces. A safe in the closet is bolted down so a thief cannot carry it off. Badge readers, fingerprint scanners, double-door entry booths, and laptop cable locks do those same jobs for offices and equipment.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small clinic keeps patient records on three front-desk laptops. Staff badge in, but visitors wait in the same open lobby. Which single physical control would most directly stop a visitor from walking out with one of those laptops?
lessons.teach:
A physical security control is any barrier, device, or procedure that limits who can physically reach a space or a piece of hardware. Four appear constantly on the exam.

A badge reader checks an electronic card or key fob before it unlocks a door. The card carries an ID, and a central system decides whether that ID may open that door at that time. Each swipe is logged, so you can audit who entered. Its weakness is that it identifies the card, not the person. A lost or shared card works for anyone.

Biometrics identify a person by a body trait, such as a fingerprint, palm, face, or iris. This fixes the shared-card problem, because the trait cannot be lent. The tradeoffs are cost, privacy concerns, and occasional false rejections of legitimate users.

A mantrap, also called an access control vestibule, is a small room with two doors. The second door will not open until the first has closed and the person inside is verified. It exists to defeat tailgating, which is following an authorized person through a door.

A cable lock is a steel cable that loops around a desk leg and locks into a laptop's security slot. It stops quick grab-and-go theft. It is not meant to stop someone with bolt cutters and time.

Worked example: a server closet keeps getting visited by people who are not on the IT team.

Step 1: install a badge reader, and review its logs. They show IT badges being used at odd hours.

Step 2: interviews reveal that badges are being borrowed. Add a fingerprint check alongside the badge, so the system confirms both the card and the person.

Step 3: the logs then show one entry while two people walked in. Install a mantrap so only one verified person passes at a time.

A common mistake is treating these controls as interchangeable. A cable lock does nothing about tailgating, and a badge reader does nothing about a laptop sitting on a lobby desk. Pick the control that matches the threat. In a running office, a mismatch leaves the real gap open while everyone believes the site is secure.

questions.prompt: A design studio lists three security problems and matches one physical control to each. Problem A: visitors slip in behind staff at the street entrance right after a staff member badges in. Control: a mantrap (an access control vestibule, a small two-door room where the inner door stays locked until the outer door has closed and the one person inside is verified). Problem B: the badge reader log for the archive room shows a designer's card opening the door on a day she was abroad, so someone else was using her card. Control: ______. Problem C: two laptops were taken from the reception desk while the receptionist was on break. Control: a cable lock (a steel cable looped around a desk leg and locked into each laptop's security slot). Which control belongs in the blank for Problem B?
choices: Install a second mantrap at the archive room door so only one person can enter at a time
Add a fingerprint check alongside the badge at the archive door so it confirms both the card and the person
Review the archive room's badge log every morning so borrowed cards are spotted faster
Attach a cable lock to the archive room's filing cabinets so they cannot be carried out
questions.why: A badge reader identifies the card, not the person, so a borrowed card still works; adding biometrics (a body-trait check like a fingerprint) confirms the actual person, which a trait that cannot be lent makes possible.

questions.prompt: A hospital pharmacy installs an access control vestibule: two doors around a small room, where the second door will not open until the first has closed and the person inside is verified. Which threat is this control mainly designed to stop?
choices: Staff sharing their fingerprint scans with coworkers
A lost badge being found and used by a stranger
Tailgating, where an unauthorized person follows an authorized one through a door
A laptop being picked up and carried out of the pharmacy
questions.why: A mantrap forces one verified person through at a time, which defeats tailgating, meaning following an authorized person through a door.

questions.prompt: A public library lends laptops that students use at open study tables. Several have vanished when students stepped away for a few minutes. Which physical control best matches this threat?
choices: A mantrap at the front door so only one person enters at a time
An iris scanner that each student must pass before entering the building
A badge reader on the library's main entrance that logs every card swipe
A cable lock looping each laptop to a table leg through its security slot
questions.why: The threat is quick grab-and-go theft of hardware sitting in the open, which is exactly what a cable lock is meant to stop; entry controls do nothing once the laptop is on a table inside.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's audit finds that warehouse staff routinely lend each other their door badges. The manager proposes putting cable locks on every desktop computer in the warehouse office. Why does this proposal fail to address the audit finding?
choices: Cable locks only work on laptops, so desktop computers cannot be secured with them at all
Cable locks replace the badge log, so the company would lose its record of who entered
Cable locks would stop the badge sharing but are too expensive compared with a mantrap
Cable locks protect hardware from quick theft but do nothing to confirm who is using a badge at the door
questions.why: The threat is shared badges, which needs a control that verifies the person, such as biometrics; a cable lock addresses hardware theft, so the mismatch leaves the real gap open.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how badge readers, biometrics, mantraps, and cable locks differ, which threat each one addresses, and at least one limit or tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer:
Each physical control blocks a different way someone gets their hands on our gear.

Badge readers unlock doors for approved cards and log every entry, which is good for auditing. But they trust the card, so a lost or loaned badge lets the wrong person in.

Biometrics check a fingerprint or face, so the credential can't be lent. They cost more, raise privacy questions, and sometimes reject real staff.

A mantrap is a two-door booth where only one verified person passes at a time. It is our answer to tailgating, but it is expensive and slows foot traffic, so we'd use it for a server room, not the break room.

Cable locks tether laptops to desks to stop quick theft in open areas. They won't stop someone determined with tools.

The point is to match the control to the threat rather than buying one and calling the site secure.
rubricPoints: Badge readers authorize cards and log entries but cannot tell who is holding the card.
Biometrics verify the person, with tradeoffs of cost, privacy, and false rejections.
A mantrap (access control vestibule) uses two doors and one-at-a-time verification to stop tailgating.
Cable locks deter opportunistic laptop theft but not a determined attacker with tools.
Controls should be chosen to match the specific threat, not applied generically.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine simulates physical access, so the most useful practice is reasoning through exam-style scenarios that match each threat to the right physical control.

lessons.plain: Logical security means the controls that live in software and settings rather than locks and walls. Four ideas carry most of the weight. Least privilege means each person or program gets only the access its job needs. Multifactor authentication means proving who you are in more than one way, such as a password plus a code from your phone. An access control list is a list that says who may do what to a file, folder or network path. Encryption scrambles data so only someone with the right key can read it. Think of an office building: a key that opens only your floor, ID plus a PIN at the door, a guest list, and sealed envelopes.
lessons.guessPrompt: An office's shared drive is protected by one strong password, and every employee knows it. If a single laptop is stolen with that password saved on it, what can the thief reach, and which change would shrink the damage most?
lessons.teach:
Least privilege is the rule that every account, user or service gets the minimum permissions needed for its task, for only as long as it needs them. It works by shrinking the blast radius, meaning how much damage one compromised account can do. A standard user account cannot install drivers, so malware running as that user cannot either.

Multifactor authentication (MFA) requires two or more different factor types. A factor is a category of proof: something you know (a password or PIN), something you have (a phone app code or hardware token), something you are (a fingerprint), and sometimes somewhere you are (location). Two passwords are still one factor. MFA works because a stolen password alone no longer unlocks the account.

An access control list (ACL) is an ordered set of entries on a resource, such as a file, folder or router interface, each saying which identity or traffic is allowed or denied which action. Most ACLs end in an implicit deny: anything not explicitly allowed is blocked.

Encryption turns readable data (plaintext) into scrambled data (ciphertext) using a key. Data at rest is stored data, such as a disk; data in transit is moving across a network, protected by protocols like HTTPS.

Worked example: a payroll folder. Step one, the ACL grants HR read and write and grants managers read only; everyone else hits the implicit deny. Step two, HR accounts require MFA, so a phished HR password still fails. Step three, the drive is encrypted at rest, so a stolen disk shows only ciphertext. Step four, an attacker who guesses a manager's password still cannot edit files.

A common mistake is adding users to an administrator group "just to make it work." In a running system that single shortcut lets one infected account rewrite permissions, disable protections and reach every file the ACLs were meant to guard.

questions.prompt: A freelance photographer hardens her own laptop and accounts. Step one: she does daily editing on a standard user account and keeps a separate administrator account only for installing software, so malware picked up while browsing cannot install drivers. Step two: her cloud backup login needs her password plus a code from a phone authenticator app, so a phished password alone fails. Step three: the laptop is stolen from a café table. [Missing step: which control keeps the thief from reading the client photos stored on its drive?] Step four: clients upload their files to her through an HTTPS site, so anyone snooping on the café Wi-Fi sees only scrambled traffic.
choices: The authenticator app code on the cloud backup, because it stops anyone using a stolen password
The standard user account, because it cannot install drivers or change system settings
Encryption at rest on the laptop's drive, so the stored files read only as ciphertext without the key
The HTTPS upload site, because it protects the photos while they move across the network
questions.why: A stolen disk is stored data, so only encryption at rest turns the photos into ciphertext the thief cannot read; HTTPS protects data in transit, and MFA and least privilege do not scramble the files on the drive.

questions.prompt: A small dental clinic wants its front-desk login to count as multifactor authentication (MFA). Which login combination actually uses two different factor types?
choices: A password followed by a second, different password
A PIN followed by a fingerprint scan
A password followed by answering a security question
A username followed by a password
questions.why: A PIN is something you know and a fingerprint is something you are, which are two different factor types; the other options use only knowledge-based proof, so they are still one factor.

questions.prompt: A café's router has an access control list (ACL) on its guest Wi-Fi interface with two entries: entry 1 allows guest devices to reach websites on the internet, and entry 2 allows guest devices to look up website names. There are no other entries. A guest laptop tries to send a print job to the office printer on the staff network. What happens?
choices: It is allowed, because the ACL contains no entry that denies printing
It is blocked, because traffic not explicitly allowed hits the implicit deny
It is allowed, because entry 1 allows guests to reach outside devices
It is allowed only if the guest has a strong Wi-Fi password
questions.why: Most ACLs end in an implicit deny, so any traffic not matched by an allow entry, like this print job, is blocked even without a written deny rule.

questions.prompt: At a small print shop, a technician adds the receptionist's account to the administrator group so a label-printing program will run. A month later the receptionist opens an infected email attachment while logged in. What is the most likely consequence of that shortcut?
choices: The malware runs with administrator rights and can rewrite permissions, disable protections and reach files the ACLs were meant to guard
The malware is limited to the receptionist's own files, because it runs as a single user
The infection is stopped automatically, because administrator accounts are scanned more strictly
Nothing extra, because ACLs on the shop's folders still block the malware no matter what group the account is in
questions.why: Breaking least privilege widens the blast radius: malware running as an administrator inherits the power to change permissions and turn off protections, so the ACLs no longer contain it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how least privilege, MFA, ACLs and encryption each stop a different part of an attack on a shared workstation, and name one tradeoff or limit of one of them.
lessons.modelAnswer: These four controls cover different gaps. MFA protects the login: a stolen password is useless without the second factor, like a phone code, but it must be a different factor type, not two passwords. Least privilege limits what a logged-in account can do, so if someone does get in, or malware runs as that user, the damage stays small. ACLs enforce that limit on specific resources by listing who can read, write or change each folder or network path, and anything not listed is denied by default. Encryption protects the data itself, at rest on the disk and in transit on the network, so a stolen drive or sniffed traffic reveals nothing without the key. The tradeoff: each adds friction. MFA slows logins, tight permissions cause help-desk tickets, and encryption means a lost key can make data unrecoverable.
rubricPoints: Least privilege grants only the minimum access needed, limiting damage from a compromised account.
MFA requires different factor types, so two passwords do not count.
ACLs list allowed or denied actions per identity on a resource and usually end in implicit deny.
Encryption protects data at rest and in transit and depends on keeping the key safe.
Names a real limit or tradeoff such as user friction or lost keys.

suggested.rationale: The unit is about choosing the right control for a given threat, so reasoning through exam-style hardening scenarios that mix all four concepts teaches more than any single existing mission.

lessons.plain: Wireless security protocols are the rules a Wi-Fi network uses to decide who may join and to scramble the radio traffic so eavesdroppers cannot read it. WPA2 and its newer replacement WPA3 handle the scrambling and the joining. Small networks usually share one password. Bigger ones give each person their own login, checked by a central server, often a RADIUS server, using a method called 802.1X. Think of an apartment building: a shared door code works until someone moves out, while a front desk checking each resident's own ID card lets you cancel just one person.
lessons.guessPrompt: An office Wi-Fi network uses one shared password that all twenty staff type in. One employee quits on bad terms. What problem does that create, and what would you need to do about it?
lessons.teach:
WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) is a wireless security standard that encrypts traffic between a device and an access point, the radio box that clients connect to. It uses AES, a strong cipher, in a mode called CCMP. WPA3 is its successor. Each comes in two flavours. Personal mode uses a pre-shared key (PSK), one passphrase that everyone types. Enterprise mode gives each user their own credentials, which a separate server checks.

WPA3-Personal replaces the PSK handshake with SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals). SAE stops an attacker who captures the handshake from guessing the passphrase offline at high speed. It also provides forward secrecy, meaning that learning the passphrase later does not unlock traffic recorded earlier. WPA2-Personal has neither protection, so a weak passphrase can be cracked from a single captured handshake.

802.1X is a standard for port-based access control: a device gets no network access until it proves its identity. It has three roles. The supplicant is the client device. The authenticator is the access point or switch. The authentication server makes the decision. RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) is the usual protocol and server for that last role. It checks credentials, often against a user directory, and replies accept or reject. The credentials travel inside EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol).

Worked example: a laptop joins a WPA2-Enterprise network. First, the laptop associates, and the access point blocks everything except authentication traffic. Second, the user enters their own username and password, which are carried in EAP. Third, the access point relays them to the RADIUS server. Fourth, RADIUS checks the account and answers accept. Fifth, the access point opens the connection and creates encryption keys unique to that user.

A common mistake is treating RADIUS or 802.1X as encryption. They decide who gets in, while WPA2 or WPA3 encrypts the air. Another is running an office on one shared PSK. When someone leaves, they still know the passphrase, and you must change it on every device. Avoid WEP and TKIP, which are broken legacy options.

questions.prompt: A public library wants only approved kiosk PCs to use its wired network. Trace the 802.1X roles as a kiosk is plugged into a wall jack. Step 1: The kiosk PC asks for access and presents its credentials, so it is the supplicant. Step 2: The network switch at the other end of the cable keeps that port closed to everything except authentication traffic and relays the kiosk's credentials onward. In 802.1X terms, the switch is acting as the ______. Step 3: A RADIUS server checks the credentials against the library's account list and answers accept or reject. Step 4: On accept, the switch opens the port; on reject, it stays closed. Which term fills the blank in Step 2?
choices: Supplicant, because the switch is the device asking to join the network
Authenticator, because the switch controls the port and relays credentials to the server
Authentication server, because the switch decides whether the kiosk is allowed in
Encryption layer, because the switch scrambles the kiosk's credentials so they cannot be read
questions.why: In 802.1X the authenticator is the access point or switch that blocks the port and passes credentials to the authentication server, which makes the actual accept or reject decision.

questions.prompt: A hotel's guest Wi-Fi uses WPA3-Personal. An attacker records guests' encrypted wireless traffic in March. In June, the attacker learns the Wi-Fi passphrase from a sign left in a lobby. What does this mean for the traffic recorded in March?
choices: It can be decrypted only if the hotel also runs a RADIUS server that stored the old keys
It was never encrypted, because Personal mode protects only the passphrase, not the traffic itself
It can now be decrypted, because anyone holding the passphrase can unlock all traffic ever sent on that network
It stays protected, because WPA3-Personal's forward secrecy means a passphrase learned later does not unlock earlier recorded traffic
questions.why: SAE in WPA3-Personal provides forward secrecy, so learning the passphrase later does not expose traffic captured before.

questions.prompt: An architecture firm has 40 staff on one shared Wi-Fi passphrase. Staff turnover is frequent, and the manager wants each person to sign in with their own credentials so that a departing employee's access can be cut off without touching anyone else's device. Which setup meets this goal?
choices: WEP with a separate passphrase written on each employee's laptop
WPA3-Enterprise, with 802.1X and a RADIUS server checking each user's own account
WPA3-Personal with a longer, more complex shared passphrase that is changed every month
WPA2-Personal using TKIP, with the passphrase printed only for current staff
questions.why: Enterprise mode gives every user individual credentials checked by a RADIUS server, so disabling one account removes only that person, whereas any shared passphrase must be changed on every device.

questions.prompt: While setting up a small accounting office, a technician says: "We've added a RADIUS server with 802.1X, so the wireless traffic is already encrypted. We can switch the access point to an open network with no WPA2 or WPA3." What is wrong with this plan?
choices: RADIUS and 802.1X decide who is allowed in, but they do not encrypt the air; WPA2 or WPA3 is still needed for that
Nothing; RADIUS encrypts each user's traffic with its own key, so WPA2 or WPA3 would only duplicate it
The plan is fine as long as the office uses EAP, because EAP is the cipher that encrypts the wireless link
802.1X only works on wired switches, so the RADIUS server will ignore wireless clients entirely
questions.why: RADIUS and 802.1X handle authentication, deciding access, while WPA2 or WPA3 provides the encryption of wireless traffic, so removing them leaves traffic unprotected.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how WPA2/WPA3 Personal differs from Enterprise with 802.1X and RADIUS, and name one tradeoff or limit that would make you choose one over the other for a small office.
lessons.modelAnswer: WPA2 and WPA3 encrypt the wireless link. Personal mode protects it with one shared passphrase, while Enterprise mode adds 802.1X. With 802.1X, the access point holds each device at the door and passes that user's own credentials, wrapped in EAP, to a RADIUS server, which says accept or reject. That means each person has their own account and their own encryption keys, so revoking one leaver means disabling one account instead of re-keying every device. WPA3 also improves Personal mode with SAE, which resists offline password guessing and gives forward secrecy. The tradeoff is effort. Enterprise needs a RADIUS server and a user directory to run and maintain, which can be too much for a tiny office. In that case, WPA3-Personal or WPA2-Personal with a long, unique passphrase is reasonable, as long as you accept rotating the passphrase whenever staff change. RADIUS controls who gets in. It does not do the encryption itself.
rubricPoints: States that WPA2/WPA3 encrypt wireless traffic, with AES as the cipher for WPA2.
Distinguishes Personal (shared pre-shared key) from Enterprise (individual credentials).
Describes 802.1X roles (supplicant, authenticator, authentication server) with RADIUS as the server.
Notes WPA3's SAE resists offline passphrase cracking and adds forward secrecy.
Names a tradeoff such as RADIUS infrastructure cost versus the hassle of rotating a shared key.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine exercises Wi-Fi authentication, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios about choosing between Personal, Enterprise, WPA2 and WPA3 builds the judgement this objective tests.

lessons.plain: Malware is software built to harm a computer or its owner. Common kinds include a virus, which spreads by riding inside other files, and ransomware, which locks your files until you pay. A trojan is disguised as something useful. A keylogger secretly records what you type, and a rootkit hides deep inside the system. Dealing with malware means spotting the signs, cleaning the machine in a careful order so the infection cannot hide or come back, and then preventing a repeat. Think of a burst pipe: shut off the water first, then dry everything out, then fix the pipe, and only then tell the household what not to do next time.
lessons.guessPrompt: You find malware on a coworker's laptop. Before you start any cleanup, what is the first physical thing you would do to that laptop to stop the problem from getting worse, and why?
lessons.teach:
Malware is any software written to harm a system or its user. A virus attaches to a legitimate file and spreads when that file runs. Ransomware encrypts files, meaning it scrambles them with a secret key, and then demands payment for that key. A trojan poses as useful software so the user installs it willingly. A keylogger records keystrokes to steal passwords. A rootkit hides inside the operating system, sometimes loading before it, so normal tools cannot see it.

You usually notice malware through symptoms. These include slowness, pop-ups, a browser homepage you never set, files that will not open, security tools that have been switched off, or odd network traffic. Anti-malware software compares files against definitions, which are fingerprints of known malware, and it also watches for suspicious behaviour.

Removal follows a fixed order:
1. Investigate and confirm the symptoms.
2. Quarantine the machine by cutting it off from the network so the malware cannot spread.
