3. Disable System Restore. This Windows feature keeps restore points, which are snapshots of system files, and those snapshots may contain the malware.
4. Remediate. Update the definitions (from clean media if the machine is offline), then scan and remove. Do this from Safe Mode, a minimal Windows startup, or from a preinstallation environment, a separate bootable system, so that hiding malware is not running.
5. Schedule regular scans and apply updates.
6. Re-enable System Restore and create a clean restore point.
7. Educate the user.

Worked example: a user installed a free PDF converter and now gets ad pages. You confirm the hijacked homepage (step 1) and unplug the network (2). You turn off System Restore (3). You boot to Safe Mode, update the definitions from a USB stick, and scan, which finds and removes a trojan (4). You schedule scans and patch the system (5), create a fresh restore point (6), and coach the user to install software only from trusted sources (7).

Common mistake: skipping step 3. A later rollback then quietly reinstalls the malware. Ransomware and stubborn rootkits are different. They usually mean reimaging, which is a full reinstall from a known-good image, followed by restoring files from offline backups.

questions.prompt: A bakery's order-taking laptop has its antivirus switched off, and the owner notices odd outbound network traffic late at night. The technician works through the removal process. Step A: confirms that the antivirus is disabled and that the strange traffic is real. Step B: [MISSING]. Step C: turns off System Restore. Step D: boots into a preinstallation environment (a separate bootable system), updates definitions from a USB stick, and scans, which finds and removes a keylogger (software that records keystrokes). Step E: schedules regular scans and applies patches. Step F: turns System Restore back on and creates a clean restore point. Step G: tells the staff to use different passwords and to avoid unknown downloads. What belongs in Step B?
choices: Reimage the laptop right away from a known-good image, before any scan is run
Connect to the shop Wi-Fi to download the newest malware definitions
Create a restore point now so the current state of the laptop is saved before anything changes
Disconnect the laptop from the network so the malware cannot spread or keep sending data
questions.why: After confirming the symptoms, the next step is to quarantine the machine by cutting it off from the network so the malware cannot spread.

questions.prompt: A technician at a law firm suspects a workstation is infected. Normal security tools show nothing wrong, but the symptoms continue. The malicious code seems to hide inside the operating system and may load before Windows starts. Which type of malware best matches this description?
choices: Trojan
Keylogger
Rootkit
Virus
questions.why: A rootkit hides inside the operating system, sometimes loading before it, so normal tools cannot see it.

questions.prompt: At a small accounting office, a staff member's workstation shows a message demanding payment. None of the spreadsheets will open because they have been scrambled with a secret key. The office keeps nightly backups on drives that are stored disconnected from the network. What is the most appropriate way to recover?
choices: Reimage the workstation from a known-good image, then restore the files from the offline backups
Pay the demand so the attacker sends the key, then update the antivirus definitions
Roll the workstation back to last week's System Restore point to undo the encryption
Run a quick scan in normal Windows and then reopen the spreadsheets
questions.why: Ransomware usually calls for reimaging, a full reinstall from a known-good image, followed by restoring files from offline backups.

questions.prompt: A technician removed a trojan from a clinic's front-desk PC but skipped disabling System Restore. Three weeks later, a user rolls the PC back to an older restore point to fix a printer driver problem, and the pop-ups immediately return. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The old restore point contained the malware, so rolling back reinstalled it
The printer driver was the trojan all along and was never scanned
The malware definitions expired, so the antivirus deleted itself
Rolling back turned the PC into Safe Mode, which allows pop-ups
questions.why: Restore points are snapshots of system files that may contain the malware, so skipping the step of disabling System Restore lets a later rollback quietly reinstall it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the order you would follow to remove malware from a Windows workstation, why disabling System Restore matters, and one situation where scanning and removing is not enough.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I confirm it really is malware by checking the symptoms, such as pop-ups, a changed homepage, or disabled antivirus. Then I quarantine the machine by pulling it off the network so it cannot spread. Next I disable System Restore, because the saved restore points may hold infected files, and rolling back later would bring the malware back. Then I update the anti-malware definitions from clean media and scan from Safe Mode or a separate boot environment, so the malware is not running while I remove it. After that I schedule scans, patch the system, turn System Restore back on, and create a clean restore point. Finally I teach the user how it happened. The limit is that a rootkit can hide from scanners, and ransomware leaves files encrypted. In those cases I reimage the machine and restore from offline backups instead of trusting a scan.
rubricPoints: Confirms the symptoms before acting, then quarantines the machine from the network.
Disables System Restore before cleaning because restore points can reinfect the system.
Updates definitions and scans from Safe Mode or a preinstallation environment.
Re-enables System Restore with a clean restore point after remediation, then schedules scans and updates.
Educates the user as the final step.
Names a limit: rootkits or ransomware often require reimaging and restoring from backups.

suggested.rationale: Hunting down and removing a hidden job that phones home makes the learner practise the core malware skills of spotting persistence, containing it, and removing it so it does not return.

lessons.plain: Social engineering means tricking a person, rather than breaking a machine, to get access or information. The attacker targets trust, helpfulness, fear or hurry. Phishing is a fake message that gets you to click, log in or pay. Shoulder surfing is watching someone type a password or read a screen. Tailgating is slipping through a secured door right behind someone who has a badge. Impersonation is pretending to be someone trusted, such as IT support, a manager or a delivery driver. Think of a con artist at a bank. They never touch the vault. They just talk the teller into opening it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A friendly stranger carrying two heavy boxes asks you to hold the badge-controlled office door for them. What could go wrong if you do, and what could you do instead?
lessons.teach:
Social engineering is any attack that manipulates people into giving up access, credentials (the usernames and passwords that prove who you are) or information. It works because people want to be helpful, respect authority, and act fast under pressure. Technical defenses like firewalls (filters that block unwanted network traffic) do nothing against it.

Phishing is a fraudulent email, text or message made to look legitimate. It pushes you to click a link, open an attachment or enter credentials on a fake page. Spear phishing targets one specific person using details about them. Whaling targets executives. Smishing is phishing by SMS text, and vishing is phishing by voice call. Shoulder surfing is reading a screen, keypad or password over someone's shoulder, sometimes from a distance or through a camera. Tailgating is following an authorized person through a controlled entrance without using your own credential. Piggybacking is the same act but with the insider's knowing consent. Impersonation is pretending to be a trusted role to get help or access.

Here is a worked example. First, a user gets an email that looks like it is from the help desk: 'Your mailbox is full, sign in here within one hour.' Second, the urgency pushes the user to click. Third, the link leads to a look-alike login page, and the user types a password. Fourth, the attacker now holds a working credential and signs in as that user. The defense is to check the sender address, hover over the link to see its real destination, and report the email instead of clicking. You can also verify any request by calling the help desk on a number you already know.

A common mistake is assuming the attacker is an obvious stranger. Impersonators wear uniforms, use real names taken from social media, and sound calm and confident. Never use contact details supplied inside a suspicious message to verify that same message.

In a running organization, one stolen password or one held door can bypass every other control. That is why user training, privacy screens, and a culture of politely challenging unbadged visitors matter.

questions.prompt: At a small veterinary clinic, the front-desk manager gets a phone call. The caller says he is from the clinic's records-software vendor and needs the remote-support code read out to him right now, or tonight's backup will fail. Step 1: Spot the warning signs. This is a voice call (vishing, or phishing by phone), the caller claims a trusted role (impersonation), and he creates time pressure. Step 2: Do not read out the code during this call, even though the caller sounds calm and knows the vendor's name. Step 3: [missing step] Step 4: If the vendor says no one called, report the attempt to whoever handles IT for the clinic, so other staff can be warned. Which action belongs in Step 3?
choices: Ask the caller for a callback number and phone him back on it, to confirm he is really with the vendor
Hang up and call the vendor's support line on the number already on file from the clinic's contract
Turn on the clinic router's firewall so the caller cannot connect to the records system remotely
Ask the caller to state his employee ID and the clinic's account number before you share anything
questions.why: You verify a request through contact details you already trust, not details the suspicious caller supplies, and an attacker could have found or made up an ID or account number.

questions.prompt: At a parts warehouse, a man in a courier jacket with no badge asks an employee to hold the secured door for him. The employee knowingly holds it open, and he walks in without using any credential of his own. Which attack term best fits?
choices: Whaling
Piggybacking
Tailgating
Shoulder surfing
questions.why: Following an authorized person through a controlled entrance with that person's knowing consent is piggybacking; tailgating is the same act without consent.

questions.prompt: Hundreds of employees at a regional credit union get the same text message: 'Dear customer, your parcel could not be delivered. Reschedule here:' followed by a short link. Which type of attack is this?
choices: Spear phishing
Whaling
Vishing
Smishing
questions.why: Phishing delivered by SMS text is smishing, and this mass, generic message targets neither one specific person nor executives.

questions.prompt: A city library's circulation desk faces the public queue. Staff often type the admin password while patrons stand a few feet behind them. Which control most directly addresses this threat?
choices: A privacy screen on the monitor and shielding the keyboard when typing
Installing updated antivirus software on the desk computer
Making staff change the admin password every 30 days
A stricter firewall rule on the library's network
questions.why: This is shoulder surfing, and blocking the view of the screen and keypad stops the observation, which network or password-rotation controls do not do.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how phishing, shoulder surfing, tailgating and impersonation differ, and name one tradeoff or limit of relying on user training to stop them.
lessons.modelAnswer: All four attacks target people instead of systems, and they exploit trust, helpfulness or urgency. Phishing uses a fake message to get someone to click, open a file or type credentials into a look-alike page. Shoulder surfing is simply watching someone enter a password or read sensitive data. Tailgating is following an authorized person through a secured door without badging in yourself. Impersonation is posing as IT, a boss or a vendor to request access or information. The defenses are mostly behavioral: verify requests through a known channel, check links before clicking, use privacy screens, and politely challenge anyone without a badge. The limit is that training fades and people still make mistakes under pressure. A tradeoff is that strict challenge rules can slow work and feel rude. Training should therefore be refreshed regularly and backed by technical controls, so that one fooled person does not mean total compromise.
rubricPoints: Defines social engineering as manipulating people rather than technology.
Correctly distinguishes phishing, shoulder surfing, tailgating and impersonation.
Names a practical countermeasure such as verifying through a known channel or challenging unbadged people.
Identifies a limit or tradeoff, such as fading training or friction for staff.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine simulates human manipulation, so recognizing these attacks and explaining the differences and defenses in your own words is the core skill.

lessons.plain: Securing a small office or home office (SOHO) network and its computers mostly comes down to three everyday habits. Password policies are house rules for passwords: how long they must be, how often they change, and what happens after too many wrong guesses. Account management means only the right people have logins, with no spare or default ones. Firewall rules decide which network traffic may come in or go out. Think of a small shop: good keys (passwords), a list of who holds keys and taking them back when staff leave (accounts), and a doorman who checks every visitor against a guest list (firewall).
lessons.guessPrompt: An office PC can be reached from the internet, and an attacker's program tries thousands of passwords per hour against it. What one account setting would most slow that attacker down, and why?
lessons.teach:
A password policy is a set of rules every account's password must meet. It covers minimum length, where longer beats cleverer and 12 or more characters is a common baseline. It covers complexity, meaning a mix of character types. History blocks reuse of recent passwords. Expiration forces a change after a set period. An account lockout threshold locks the account for a while after a number of wrong guesses. Lockout works because brute forcing, which means guessing passwords one after another, needs thousands of tries, and lockout caps the attacker at a handful.

Account management means controlling which accounts exist and what each can do. Disable the built-in Guest account. Rename or disable the default Administrator. Give each person their own standard, non-admin account. Disable accounts the day someone leaves. Require a screen lock after a few idle minutes. Change every default password, especially the router's, because factory credentials are published online.

A firewall is a filter that checks each network connection against an ordered list of rules, then allows or blocks it. Rules are read top to bottom and the first match wins. Anything that matches no rule hits an implicit deny. A port is a numbered door for a service, such as 443 for HTTPS web traffic or 3389 for Remote Desktop.

Worked example: a SOHO router has two rules. Rule 1 allows inbound TCP 443 to 192.168.1.20, the office web server. It is reached through port forwarding, which passes outside traffic to one inside device. Rule 2 denies all other inbound traffic. A connection arrives for port 3389. Rule 1 checks for port 443 and does not match. Rule 2 matches everything, so the connection is blocked. A connection to port 443 matches rule 1 and is forwarded.

A common mistake is forwarding Remote Desktop to the internet for convenience. Another is leaving UPnP (Universal Plug and Play) enabled, since it lets devices open ports on their own. Either one exposes a login screen to automated guessing worldwide, and without lockout an attacker can eventually get in.

questions.prompt: A small bakery's router has two inbound rules. Rule 1 allows inbound TCP 8443 to 10.0.0.15, the bakery's online ordering server. Rule 2 denies inbound TCP 22. No other rules are listed. A connection arrives from the internet for port 5900, a port used by a remote-control tool. Step 1: Rule 1 checks for port 8443. 5900 is not 8443, so there is no match. Step 2: Rule 2 checks for port 22. 5900 is not 22, so there is no match. Step 3: ______. What is the missing Step 3?
choices: The connection is forwarded to 10.0.0.15, because that is the only inside device with a forwarding rule
No rule matched, so the connection hits the implicit deny and is blocked
The router goes back to Rule 1 and checks again, because the firewall must find a match before deciding
The connection is allowed, because no listed rule specifically denies port 5900
questions.why: Traffic that matches no rule in the list falls to the implicit deny, so the port 5900 connection is blocked even though no rule names it.

questions.prompt: An attacker runs a script against the login of a bookkeeping firm's file server. The script tries one password after another for the account "jlee". Which password policy setting most directly limits the attacker to only a handful of guesses?
choices: Password history set to remember the last 10 passwords
Password expiration set to force a change every 90 days
Account lockout threshold set to lock the account after 5 wrong attempts
Complexity rules that require upper case, lower case, numbers and symbols
questions.why: Brute forcing needs thousands of tries, and a lockout threshold locks the account after a few wrong guesses, which caps the attacker at a handful.

questions.prompt: At a veterinary clinic, the four front-desk staff all sign in to the reception PC with one shared account that has administrator rights. Which change best follows account management best practice?
choices: Enable the built-in Guest account so staff do not need to use the administrator account
Rename the shared administrator account so it is harder to guess, and keep everyone using it
Give each staff member their own standard, non-admin account
Give the shared administrator account a longer password and tell only the four staff
questions.why: Each person should have their own standard, non-admin account, so activity is tied to one person and everyday use does not run with administrator rights.

questions.prompt: A landscaping company's router has these inbound rules in this order. Rule 1 denies all inbound traffic. Rule 2 allows inbound TCP 443 to 172.16.0.40, the company's web server. A customer's browser connects to the web server on port 443. What happens?
choices: The connection is blocked, because Rule 1 matches first and the first match wins
The connection is blocked by the implicit deny, because no rule matched
The connection is allowed, because allow rules are always checked before deny rules
The connection is allowed, because Rule 2 is more specific than Rule 1
questions.why: Rules are read top to bottom and the first match wins, so the deny-all rule at the top blocks the connection before the allow rule is ever checked.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how password policy, account management and firewall rules together protect a small office PC from an internet password-guessing attack, and name one tradeoff or limit of account lockout.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each layer covers a different gap. First, the firewall should block the attack before it starts. The router reads its rules top to bottom, and anything not explicitly allowed hits the implicit deny. So we only forward the ports we truly need, such as 443 to the web server, never Remote Desktop, and we turn off UPnP so devices can't open ports themselves. Second, if a login is still reachable, the password policy makes guessing slow. Long passwords are hard to guess, and the lockout threshold stops an attacker after a few wrong tries. Third, account management shrinks the targets. We disable Guest, rename or disable the default admin, remove leavers' accounts, and change the router's default password. The tradeoff with lockout is that an attacker can deliberately trigger it to lock real users out, which causes help desk calls and downtime. So we pick a sensible threshold and a timed unlock.
rubricPoints: States that firewall rules are evaluated in order, first match wins, with an implicit deny at the end.
Recommends forwarding only needed ports and avoiding exposed Remote Desktop or UPnP.
Explains that length and lockout thresholds defeat brute-force guessing.
Lists account hygiene: disable Guest, handle default admin, remove unused accounts, change default router passwords.
Names a real limit, such as lockout being abused to deny service to legitimate users.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this through hardening scenarios where the learner must pick the specific control that fits the threat, so reasoning through situations adds the most.

lessons.plain: A phone or tablet holds email, photos, work files and saved logins, and it is easy to lose. Securing it means three layers. A screen lock is the front-door lock: a PIN, password, pattern or fingerprint needed before anyone can use the device. Full-device encryption scrambles everything stored on it so the data is unreadable without the unlock secret, even if someone pulls out the storage chip. Remote wipe is a self-destruct button you press from another computer to erase the device once it is gone. Think of a locked safe that you can also order to empty itself from far away.
lessons.guessPrompt: An employee leaves a company phone in a taxi. It has a 4-digit PIN but no encryption, and nobody can reach it remotely. What could a determined finder still get at, and what one extra control would you most want in place?
lessons.teach:
Mobile and embedded devices (phones, tablets, and small single-purpose gadgets such as smart cameras or handheld scanners) are easy to lose and steal, so their protection assumes the attacker will have the device in hand.

A screen lock requires something before the device can be used: a PIN (a short number), a password, a swipe pattern, or biometrics (fingerprint or face). Good settings add an auto-lock timeout, so an idle device locks itself, and a failed-attempt limit that delays further tries or erases the device after too many wrong guesses. That limit is what makes a short PIN workable.

Full-device encryption scrambles all stored data with a key tied to the unlock secret. Without the correct PIN or password, the stored data is meaningless. A lock alone only blocks the normal screen. Encryption also protects against someone who removes the storage or reads it with special tools.

Remote wipe is erasing the device over the network from a web console or a mobile device management (MDM) system. MDM is a central service an organization uses to enforce settings, such as requiring a lock and encryption, and to locate, lock or wipe enrolled devices. Locator apps offer the same idea for personal devices.

Worked example: a technician's tablet is stolen. Step 1: the thief meets a 6-digit lock. Step 2: guessing triggers delays, then a wipe after 10 failures. Step 3: the thief removes the storage, but encryption makes it unreadable. Step 4: IT sends a remote wipe from MDM. It runs the moment the tablet reaches the network. Step 5: IT revokes the user's saved credentials as well.

Common mistake: relying on remote wipe alone. A wipe only works if the device gets online, and a thief can keep it offline. Encryption and the lock must already be in place. The consequence is that one lost device can leak customer data and company logins.

questions.prompt: A small dental clinic is setting up its three front-desk phones through its mobile device management (MDM) service, a central system that pushes required settings to enrolled devices. Staff want a quick 4-digit PIN. The office manager works through the policy: (1) Require a screen lock with a 4-digit PIN, since staff unlock the phones dozens of times a day. (2) Set an auto-lock timeout of 1 minute, so a phone left on the counter locks itself. (3) ??? (4) Turn on full-device encryption, so patient data stored on the phone is unreadable without the PIN, even if the storage is removed. Which setting belongs in step 3 so that a short 4-digit PIN is still reasonably safe?
choices: Set a failed-attempt limit that adds delays and erases the phone after too many wrong PINs
Turn off biometrics so the PIN is the only way to unlock the phone
Lengthen the auto-lock timeout to 15 minutes so staff are interrupted less often
Rely on a remote wipe from MDM as the protection against PIN guessing
questions.why: A failed-attempt limit stops a thief from trying all 10,000 four-digit combinations, which is what makes a short PIN workable.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's handheld barcode scanner has a screen lock but no full-device encryption. A thief opens the case and reads the storage chip with a special reader. What happens to the stored data?
choices: It can be read, because a lock only blocks the normal screen and does not protect the stored data
It can be read only if the thief also guesses the PIN
It is safe, because the failed-attempt limit erases the chip once it is removed
It is safe, because the screen lock also scrambles the stored files
questions.why: Without encryption, the lock only guards the normal way into the device. Data read straight from the storage is not scrambled.

questions.prompt: An architect's personal phone, not enrolled in her employer's mobile device management (MDM) system, is left in a taxi. She wants to erase it over the network. Which option fits this situation?
choices: Ask her employer's IT team to wipe it from the MDM console
Turn on full-device encryption remotely now that it is lost
Use the phone's locator app or the vendor's web console to send a remote wipe
Wait for the failed-attempt limit to erase it, since that is the same as a remote wipe
questions.why: MDM can only act on enrolled devices. For personal devices, a locator app or web console offers the same locate, lock and wipe idea.

questions.prompt: A retail chain's security plan for its store tablets says: 'If a tablet is stolen, we will remote-wipe it, so no lock or encryption is needed.' A thief keeps a stolen tablet switched off and away from any network. What is the result?
choices: The wipe runs anyway, because MDM commands do not need a network connection
The data is safe because MDM encrypts the tablet the moment it is reported stolen
The wipe never runs, so the unlocked and unencrypted data can be read freely
The tablet erases itself after 10 minutes offline
questions.why: A remote wipe only works once the device gets online. A lock and encryption must already be in place to protect a device kept offline.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how screen locks, full-device encryption and remote wipe work together on a lost company phone, and name one limit of remote wipe.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each control covers a different gap, so we use all three. The screen lock stops a finder from just opening the phone. With an auto-lock timeout and a failed-attempt limit, even a short PIN can't be brute-forced, because guesses get delayed or the phone erases itself. Full-device encryption means the stored data is scrambled with a key tied to the unlock secret, so pulling the storage out or using forensic tools gets nothing readable. Remote wipe, usually sent from our MDM console, erases the phone after we know it's gone. The limit is that a wipe only happens when the device reaches a network. A thief who keeps it in airplane mode or a shielded bag blocks it. That's why the lock and encryption have to be enforced ahead of time. We should also reset the user's passwords and tokens after any loss.
rubricPoints: A screen lock with auto-lock timeout and a failed-attempt limit blocks casual and guessing access.
Full-device encryption keeps data unreadable even if the storage is removed or bypassed.
Remote wipe erases the device from a central console such as MDM or a locator service.
Remote wipe needs the device to come online, so it cannot be the only control.
Controls must be enforced before loss, and credentials should be revoked after it.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine covers mobile device hardening, so reasoning through lost-device scenarios that call for choosing lock, encryption and wipe settings best matches the exam's question style.

lessons.plain: Windows ships with several built-in guards, each aimed at a different danger. Microsoft Defender Antivirus scans files and programs for malicious software. Windows Defender Firewall decides which network traffic may enter or leave the computer. BitLocker scrambles (encrypts) a whole drive so a stolen disk is unreadable without the right key. User Account Control (UAC) makes even an administrator work with ordinary rights and asks for confirmation before anything changes the system. Think of a house: a guard checks who comes in, the door lock follows a guest list, a safe protects valuables if burglars get in, and someone asks 'are you sure?' before furniture moves.
lessons.guessPrompt: A laptop with antivirus and the firewall both switched on is left in a taxi. Does either of those two protect the files on its drive from whoever finds it? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Each Windows control answers one specific threat, so hardening means matching control to threat.

Microsoft Defender Antivirus is the built-in malware scanner. Real-time protection checks files as they are opened, and definition updates teach it about new threats. It protects a running system against malicious code.

Windows Defender Firewall filters network traffic using rules. An inbound rule controls connections arriving at the PC; an outbound rule controls connections the PC starts. Rules can differ by network profile: Domain (a corporate network with a domain controller), Private (a trusted home network) and Public (untrusted networks like a cafe), where the strictest settings belong.

BitLocker is full-volume encryption: everything on the drive is stored scrambled. It normally keeps its key in the TPM (Trusted Platform Module, a security chip on the motherboard) and also produces a recovery key, a long number used if the TPM check fails. BitLocker To Go encrypts removable drives. BitLocker is available on Pro, Enterprise and Education editions, not Home.

UAC runs programs with standard rights until elevation is needed. An administrator sees a consent prompt (Yes/No); a standard user sees a credential prompt asking for an admin password.

Worked example: a sales rep's laptop. Threat one, theft: enable BitLocker, then store the recovery key somewhere other than the laptop. Threat two, cafe Wi-Fi: confirm that network is set to the Public profile so unsolicited inbound connections are blocked. Threat three, a malicious download: keep Defender real-time protection and updates on. Threat four, that download trying to install itself: give the rep a standard account so UAC demands an admin password.

Common mistake: assuming BitLocker stops malware. Once the user unlocks and logs in, the data is readable to any program running as that user; encryption only protects data at rest, such as a powered-off or stolen device. The other trap is losing the recovery key: after a motherboard swap or TPM change, the data is permanently unrecoverable.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic hardens its front-desk PC, which runs Windows 11 Pro. The office manager names the threats and the controls chosen so far. Threat A: the PC itself could be stolen overnight. Control: BitLocker on the internal drive, with the recovery key printed and locked in the owner's safe. Threat B: the receptionist might download a fake invoice that carries malware. Control: Defender real-time protection on, with definition updates current. Threat C: that malware might try to install software system-wide. Control: the receptionist uses a standard account, so UAC asks for an admin password. Threat D: every evening the receptionist carries a USB stick of patient X-rays to the branch office, and the stick could be lost on the bus. Which control completes Threat D?
choices: Run a Defender scan on the USB stick before it leaves the clinic each evening
Turn on BitLocker for the PC's internal drive, because that drive is already being encrypted
Add an outbound firewall rule that blocks the PC from sending files to the branch office
Encrypt the USB stick with BitLocker To Go so a lost stick's contents stay scrambled
questions.why: A lost removable drive is a data-at-rest theft risk on that drive, and BitLocker To Go is the control that encrypts removable drives.

questions.prompt: At a public library, a patron logged in with a standard (non-administrator) account tries to install a printer driver that needs elevated rights. With User Account Control (UAC) on its usual settings, what does the patron see?
choices: A consent prompt with Yes and No buttons, so the patron can approve the install themselves
No prompt at all, because UAC only watches administrator accounts
A Defender warning that the driver has been quarantined as malware
A credential prompt asking for an administrator's password before the install can continue
questions.why: UAC shows standard users a credential prompt that asks for an admin password. Only administrators get the simpler Yes/No consent prompt.

questions.prompt: A small architecture firm sends a technician to replace the failed motherboard in a BitLocker-encrypted workstation. When the machine boots, it asks for the BitLocker recovery key. Nobody ever saved that key anywhere. What is the outcome for the data on the drive?
choices: The new motherboard's TPM automatically picks up the old key, so the data unlocks after a reboot
The data is permanently unrecoverable, because the TPM check failed and the recovery key is lost
Defender can decrypt the drive because it has full access to the files
The technician can unlock the drive by signing in with the user's normal Windows password
questions.why: After a motherboard or TPM change, the recovery key is the only way to unlock a BitLocker drive. Without it, the encrypted data cannot be read again.

questions.prompt: A bakery owner wants to stop a recipe-management app on the shop PC from connecting out to the internet, while leaving everything else alone. Which Windows Defender Firewall setting fits this goal?
choices: Switching the shop's network from the Private profile to the Domain profile
An inbound rule that blocks connections arriving at the PC for that app
An outbound rule that blocks connections that app starts
Turning on BitLocker so the app's data cannot leave the drive
questions.why: Outbound rules control the connections the PC itself starts, and an app reaching out to the internet is exactly that kind of connection.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Defender Antivirus, the Windows firewall, BitLocker and UAC each protect a laptop, and name one thing each one does not protect against.
lessons.modelAnswer: They cover different threats, so you need all four. Defender Antivirus scans files in real time for known malware, but it can miss brand-new threats if definitions are stale, and it does nothing for a stolen drive. The firewall filters inbound and outbound connections by profile, so on public Wi-Fi it should use the Public profile; it cannot stop a user from opening an infected attachment. BitLocker encrypts the whole drive, keyed by the TPM, so a thief pulling the disk sees only scrambled data; once the user is logged in, though, files are readable to any program they run, and if the recovery key is lost the data is gone. UAC keeps admins at standard rights and prompts before system changes; it only helps if users are not trained to click Yes automatically, which is why standard accounts with a credential prompt are stronger.
rubricPoints: Defender Antivirus detects and blocks malware on a running system and needs current definitions.
The firewall filters inbound and outbound traffic, with the Public profile strictest for untrusted networks.
BitLocker encrypts data at rest using the TPM and needs a safely stored recovery key.
BitLocker does not protect data once the system is unlocked and in use.
UAC runs tasks with standard rights and prompts for consent or credentials before elevation.
Each control is matched to a specific threat rather than enabled generically.

suggested.rationale: No existing mission or planned engine configures Windows controls, so reasoning through exam-style hardening scenarios that match each control to a threat builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Troubleshooting common Windows problems means working out why a computer is slow, why a program keeps closing, why the machine will not start, or why it suddenly shows a blue error screen and restarts. Instead of guessing, you gather clues, form a theory, test the least risky fix first, and check the result. It is like a mechanic with a car that makes a strange noise. They do not replace the engine first. They listen, ask what changed recently, check the simple things, and only then take bigger steps. Most Windows faults trace back to a recent change, a bad driver, failing hardware or damaged system files.
lessons.guessPrompt: A user says their laptop started showing blue error screens the day after they installed a new graphics card driver. What would you try first, and why?
lessons.teach:
Windows troubleshooting is a structured way to find and fix four common faults: slow performance, application crashes, boot failures and blue screen errors. The key habit is to ask what changed recently and to try the least destructive fix first.

Slow performance: open Task Manager, the built-in tool that shows which processes (running programs) are using CPU, memory and disk. A process stuck near 100 percent, or a nearly full disk, is the usual suspect. Also check startup programs that launch at sign-in.

Application crashes: Event Viewer is the Windows log viewer, and its Application log records which program failed and the faulting file. Fixes include updating or repairing the app, or reinstalling it.

Boot failures: when Windows will not start, use the Windows Recovery Environment (WinRE), a separate repair mode that offers Startup Repair (automatic boot fixes), System Restore (rolling system settings back to an earlier snapshot called a restore point) and a command prompt. Safe Mode starts Windows with only basic drivers, which tells you whether a third-party driver or program is to blame.

Blue screen errors, called BSOD (blue screen of death), show a stop code naming the type of failure. Most are caused by drivers, the small programs that let Windows talk to hardware, or by failing memory or disks.

Worked example: a BSOD appears after a graphics driver update. Step one, note the stop code. Step two, boot into Safe Mode; if it is stable, a driver is likely. Step three, in Device Manager use Roll Back Driver. Step four, restart normally and confirm no further crashes. If damaged system files are suspected, the System File Checker (sfc /scannow) repairs them.

Common mistake: jumping straight to reinstalling Windows. That wipes settings and wastes hours when a driver rollback would have worked. In a running business, the user loses data and working time for no reason.

questions.prompt: At a small bakery, the point-of-sale app on the front-counter PC started closing without warning every time a receipt is printed. The technician works through it like this. Step one: ask what changed recently. The owner says the app installed an update last night. Step two: [missing]. Step three: the record names a receipt-printing add-on file that belongs to the app, so the technician runs the app's built-in repair option. Step four: print three test receipts and confirm the app stays open. Which action best fills step two?
choices: Open Device Manager and use Roll Back Driver on the display adapter
Reinstall Windows so the update and any damage it caused are completely removed
Open Task Manager and end every process using more than 10 percent of the CPU
Open Event Viewer and read the Application log entry for the crash to find the faulting file
questions.why: Event Viewer is the Windows log viewer, and its Application log records which program failed and the faulting file, which is exactly the information step three relies on.

questions.prompt: A desktop at a veterinary office crashes with a blue screen several times a day. The technician starts it in Safe Mode, and it runs all afternoon without a single crash. What does this result most likely suggest?
choices: A third-party driver or program that loads during a normal start is likely causing the crashes
Windows itself is damaged beyond repair and has to be reinstalled
The crashes come from a single app, so its entry in the Application log is the only thing to check
The hard disk is full and must be replaced before Windows will start normally
questions.why: Safe Mode starts Windows with only basic drivers, so stability there points to an extra driver or program that loads in a normal start.

questions.prompt: An office assistant at a law firm says her laptop has become very slow over the past week, even when she has only a web browser open. Which tool should a technician open first to see which running programs are using the CPU, memory and disk?
choices: Device Manager
Task Manager
System Restore in the Windows Recovery Environment
Event Viewer
questions.why: Task Manager is the built-in tool that shows which processes are using CPU, memory and disk, which is where slow-performance troubleshooting starts.

questions.prompt: At a print shop, a PC begins showing blue screen errors the day after a new network card driver is installed. The technician immediately wipes the drive and reinstalls Windows. Why is this the wrong approach?
choices: A reinstall should only be done from Safe Mode, never from the Windows Recovery Environment
It skips the less destructive fixes, such as rolling back the new driver, and costs the user settings, data and hours of work
Blue screens are always caused by failing memory, so a reinstall cannot fix them
The stop code has to be cleared with System File Checker before Windows can be reinstalled
questions.why: Good troubleshooting asks what changed and tries the least destructive fix first. Here a driver rollback would probably have worked without wiping settings or wasting the user's working time.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would approach a Windows PC that keeps blue-screening, in your own words, and name one limit or tradeoff of the tools you would use.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by asking what changed recently, such as a new driver, an update or new hardware, and I write down the stop code from the blue screen. Then I boot into Safe Mode, which loads only basic drivers. If the PC is stable there, a third-party driver or program is the likely cause, so I roll back or update that driver in Device Manager. If it will not boot at all, I use the Windows Recovery Environment for Startup Repair or System Restore. I check Event Viewer for related errors and run System File Checker if system files may be damaged. Reinstalling Windows is the last resort. A tradeoff: System Restore only rolls back system settings and programs to a restore point, so it can remove apps installed since then, and it does not help if no restore point exists or the cause is failing hardware.
rubricPoints: Starts by asking what changed recently and noting the stop code or symptom.
Uses Safe Mode to separate driver or software causes from core Windows problems.
Names a specific fix such as rolling back a driver, Startup Repair or System Restore.
Uses logs like Event Viewer or tools like Task Manager to gather evidence.
Treats reinstalling Windows as a last resort.
Names a real limit, such as System Restore needing a restore point or not fixing hardware faults.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing the right Windows tool and order of steps for a described symptom, so reasoning through scenario questions builds the skill best, since no listed mission uses Windows.

lessons.plain: Some security problems announce themselves through odd browser behavior. Browser redirection means you type one web address or search and land somewhere you never asked for. Unwanted pop-ups are windows or alerts that keep appearing, often ads or fake warnings. Rogue antivirus is a fake security program that shouts that your PC is badly infected and demands payment to fix it, when it is the real problem. Think of a house where the street signs have been swapped, flyers keep getting pushed under the door, and a stranger in a uniform says the wiring is dangerous and wants cash. Each one is a clue that something unwanted has moved in.
lessons.guessPrompt: A user says that every time they search in their web browser, they land on an unfamiliar search site full of ads, and it happens in every browser on the PC. Is the problem more likely inside one browser or somewhere in the computer's wider settings, and why?
lessons.teach:
These three symptoms usually point to unwanted software, called malware, or to its milder cousin, adware (software that exists to push ads at you).

Browser redirection comes from a browser hijacker, which is software that changes where the browser sends you. It may change the homepage or default search engine, or add a browser extension, which is a small add-on that runs inside the browser. At the system level it may edit the hosts file, a local text file that Windows checks before DNS. DNS is the service that turns names like example.com into network addresses. It may also set a proxy, which is a middleman server that all web traffic passes through.

Unwanted pop-ups come from adware, malicious extensions, or websites the user allowed to send notifications. Notifications are alerts a site can push even when you are not on it.

Rogue antivirus, also called scareware, is a fake security tool. It shows alarming scan results to frighten the user into paying or installing more malware.

Worked example: searches land on an ad-filled site. Step one, check whether a second browser does the same. It does, so the cause is probably system-wide rather than one browser. Step two, inspect the proxy settings, then the hosts file, then the DNS server settings. Step three, you find an unknown proxy and a recently installed program you do not recognize. Step four, treat this as a confirmed infection and hand off to the formal malware-removal procedure. If only one browser had been affected, you would review its extensions and reset its search settings instead.

A common mistake is fixing only the visible symptom, such as resetting the homepage, or clicking the rogue antivirus's own 'remove threats' button. The real program survives, so the redirection returns. Worse, the user may hand over card details or let in more malware, and typed passwords may be captured. Unexplained redirects, pop-ups, or fake security alerts should always be treated as signs of an infection that needs proper removal.

questions.prompt: At a small accounting firm, an employee reports that every search typed into Firefox lands on an unfamiliar, ad-heavy search page. The technician works through it. Step 1: On the same PC, the technician opens Edge and runs the same search. Edge returns normal results. Step 2: ______. Step 3: In Firefox's add-ons list, the technician finds an extension called 'QuickCoupons' that the employee does not remember installing. The technician removes it and resets Firefox's default search engine. Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: Conclude the cause is system-wide, so start by inspecting the PC's proxy settings and hosts file
Conclude Edge is the infected browser, since it was not showing the redirect, and reset Edge first
Conclude the problem is probably limited to Firefox, so focus on Firefox's extensions and search settings
Conclude the problem is caused by the DNS server, since searches are failing, and change it
questions.why: Only one browser misbehaved, so the cause is most likely inside that browser, such as an extension or its search settings, rather than a system-wide setting like the proxy, hosts file or DNS.

questions.prompt: A warehouse clerk's PC suddenly shows a window titled 'PC Shield Ultimate' that the company never installed. It reports 63 critical infections and offers to remove them for $49.99, with a large 'Remove Threats Now' button. What is the best way to respond?
choices: Pay the fee with a company card, then run a second scan to confirm the threats are gone
Close the window and reset the browser homepage, since that removes the fake tool
Treat it as rogue antivirus that signals an infection, avoid its buttons, and follow proper malware removal
Click 'Remove Threats Now' so the tool can clean the 63 infections it found
questions.why: This is scareware, a fake security tool; its own button and payment page only lead to more malware or stolen card details, so it must be handled as a real infection.

questions.prompt: A teacher's laptop keeps showing small ad pop-ups in the corner of the screen from a recipe website, even when that website is not open in any tab. Extensions look clean, and the teacher remembers clicking 'Allow' on that site some weeks ago. What is the most likely cause?
choices: A proxy server is routing all web traffic through the recipe site
The default search engine was changed to the recipe site's search page
The recipe site was given permission to send notifications, which can appear even when the site is not open
The hosts file was edited to send other site names to the recipe site
questions.why: Notifications are alerts a site can push even when you are not visiting it, and clicking 'Allow' grants that permission.

questions.prompt: At a car dealership, a salesperson's PC sends web searches in both Chrome and Edge to an ad-filled site. A technician resets the homepage and search engine in both browsers, and searches work again. Two days later, the redirect is back in both browsers. What best explains this?
choices: The browsers were reset in the wrong order, so the settings in the second browser overwrote the first
The ad site changed its address, so the browser resets no longer block it
The underlying program, such as one that set a proxy or edited the hosts file, was never removed, so it reapplied the changes
Resetting the search engine always needs a reboot, and the PC was not restarted afterwards
questions.why: Fixing only the visible symptom leaves the hijacking software in place, and a problem affecting both browsers points to a system-wide cause that needs proper malware removal.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell whether a browser redirection problem lives in one browser or in the whole system, and name one limit of simply resetting the browser.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I'd open a different browser and try the same search. If only one browser redirects, the cause is probably inside it: a hijacked homepage or search setting, or a bad extension. I'd review its extensions and reset its settings. If every browser redirects, the change is system-wide. Then I'd check the proxy settings, the hosts file, which Windows checks before DNS, and the DNS server settings, and look for recently installed programs I don't recognize. The limit of just resetting the browser is that it treats the symptom. If a hijacker program or a rogue antivirus is still installed, it will change the settings back, keep pushing pop-ups, and may steal passwords. So once I've confirmed malware, I follow the full malware-removal procedure rather than stopping at the reset. I also never click the fake scanner's own 'fix' button.
rubricPoints: Tests a second browser to separate a browser-level cause from a system-level one.
Names browser-level causes such as extensions or a changed homepage or search engine.
Names system-level causes such as the hosts file, the proxy, or DNS settings.
Recognizes rogue antivirus as fake software and never uses its own fix or payment prompt.
States that resetting settings alone is a symptom fix and the infection can return.
Hands confirmed malware off to the formal removal procedure.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or engine covers Windows browser symptoms, so reasoning through exam-style user scenarios best builds the skill of mapping each symptom to its likely cause and next step.

lessons.plain: Malware removal is the cleanup job you do when a computer has caught malicious software, meaning programs built to spy, steal, or do damage. Good technicians follow a fixed order instead of deleting the first odd file they see. Think of treating a contagious patient. First confirm the illness. Then isolate the patient so others stay safe. Throw away contaminated backups. Treat the illness thoroughly. Book follow-up checkups. Make a clean new backup. Finally, teach the patient how to avoid catching it again. Skipping or reordering steps lets the infection spread or come straight back.
lessons.guessPrompt: You suspect a laptop has a virus. Should you disconnect it from the office network before or after you start scanning and deleting files, and why?
lessons.teach:
The best-practice malware removal procedure is a seven-step sequence. Learn the steps in this order.

First, investigate and verify the symptoms. Confirm it really is malware and not a hardware fault or a bad update. Second, quarantine the system. Quarantine here means isolating the machine, usually by unplugging the network cable and turning off Wi-Fi, so the malware cannot spread or send data out. Third, disable System Restore, which Windows calls System Protection. This is a feature that saves restore points, which are snapshots of system files and settings. Those snapshots can hold the malware, so they must be cleared. Fourth, remediate, meaning remove the infection. Update the anti-malware software so its definitions, the signatures it uses to recognise threats, are current. Then scan and remove. If the malware resists, scan from Safe Mode, a startup mode that loads only essential drivers, or from a preinstallation environment, a small separate operating system booted from a USB stick or disc. Fifth, schedule regular scans and run operating system and application updates. Sixth, re-enable System Restore and create a fresh, clean restore point. Seventh, educate the end user about how the infection probably happened.

Worked example: a user's PC shows pop-ups and runs slowly. You check it and confirm a known adware program (step 1). You pull the network cable (step 2). You turn off System Protection, which deletes the old restore points (step 3). You update definitions offline from a USB stick, boot into Safe Mode and remove the adware (step 4). You set a weekly scan and install pending patches (step 5). You turn protection back on and create a restore point (step 6). You explain to the user that the free download they installed carried the adware (step 7).

A common mistake is leaving System Restore on. A user, or Windows itself, later rolls back to an infected restore point and the malware returns. Another mistake is scanning while the machine is still on the network, which lets the infection reach other computers.

questions.prompt: A technician at a small accounting firm gets a laptop whose browser home page keeps switching to an unknown search site. Step 1: she confirms it is a browser hijacker and not a faulty extension update. Step 2: she unplugs the Ethernet cable and turns off Wi-Fi. Step 3: MISSING. Step 4: she copies current definitions from a USB stick and scans. The hijacker resists, so she boots a preinstallation environment from USB and removes it. Step 5: she sets a daily scan and installs pending OS and application updates. Step 6: she turns System Protection back on and creates a new restore point. Step 7: she explains that a pirated browser plugin most likely carried the hijacker. What is the missing step 3?
choices: Turn off System Protection so the old restore points are deleted
Reconnect to the network briefly to download the newest definitions
Run a full scan right away using the existing, out-of-date definitions
Create a restore point now so the current state can be recovered later
questions.why: Step 3 is disabling System Restore (System Protection), which clears restore points that may hold the hijacker before remediation begins.

questions.prompt: In the best-practice malware removal procedure, what does it mean to quarantine the system?
choices: Moving suspicious files into the anti-malware tool's holding folder
Cutting the machine off from all networks, wired and wireless
Booting into Safe Mode so only essential drivers are loaded
Rolling the machine back to its most recent restore point
questions.why: Quarantine in this procedure means isolating the machine from the network so the malware cannot spread or send data out.

questions.prompt: At a warehouse, a technician has confirmed a trojan on a shipping kiosk PC, isolated it, disabled System Restore, and removed the trojan. She has also scheduled weekly scans and installed all pending updates. What should she do next?
choices: Disable System Restore again to clear any remaining snapshots
Explain to the kiosk's users how the infection probably happened
Re-enable System Restore and create a fresh, clean restore point
Disconnect the kiosk from the network to stop the trojan spreading
questions.why: After scheduling scans and updating comes re-enabling System Restore with a clean restore point, and user education follows that.

questions.prompt: At a school library, a technician removed spyware from a PC but never disabled System Restore. Two weeks later, Windows rolled back to an earlier restore point after a failed update, and the spyware was back. What is the most likely reason?
choices: The scan should have been run with the PC still connected to the network
The spyware was hiding in a driver that Safe Mode had failed to load
Infected restore points survived, and the rollback restored the spyware
Outdated definitions let part of the spyware survive the original scan
questions.why: Leaving System Restore on keeps old restore points that can contain the malware, so rolling back to one brings the infection back.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the seven malware removal steps in order, why System Restore is turned off and later back on, and one tradeoff or limit of this procedure.
lessons.modelAnswer: First we confirm the symptoms really are malware. Then we quarantine the PC by cutting its network access so the malware can't spread or send data out. Next we disable System Restore, because old restore points may contain the infection and could bring it back. Then we remediate: update the anti-malware definitions, then scan and remove, using Safe Mode or a bootable preinstallation environment if the malware fights back. After that we schedule scans and apply updates. Then we re-enable System Restore and make a clean restore point, so future rollbacks start from a healthy state. Last, we teach the user how the infection got in. The tradeoff is that disabling System Restore deletes every older restore point, so any legitimate rollback options are lost. Isolating the machine also means the user can't work for a while.
rubricPoints: Lists the seven steps in the correct order, from verifying symptoms to educating the user.
Explains that quarantine means isolating the machine from the network to stop spread.
Explains that restore points can hold malware, so System Restore is disabled before cleaning.
Mentions updating definitions before scanning, and using Safe Mode or a preinstallation environment for stubborn malware.
Explains that System Restore is re-enabled afterward with a new clean restore point.
Names a tradeoff, such as losing older restore points or user downtime.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission walks through Windows malware removal, and the exam tests this as putting steps in order inside a scenario, so reasoning through exam-style situations adds the most.

lessons.plain: When a phone or tablet misbehaves, three everyday complaints come up most: it has no signal, an app will not open, or its data (email, contacts, photos) stops matching what is on the computer or in the cloud. Troubleshooting these means checking the simple, likely causes first, like a switch left off, a full storage space, or an expired password, before trying anything drastic. Think of it like a car that will not start: you check whether it has fuel and the key is turned before you rebuild the engine. The goal is to fix the problem with the smallest, safest change.
lessons.guessPrompt: A user says their phone suddenly shows no Wi-Fi and no cellular bars at the same moment, even though coworkers nearby are fine. What single setting would you check first, and why?
lessons.teach:
Mobile troubleshooting means finding why a phone or tablet stops connecting, launching apps, or keeping data matched with other devices, and fixing it with the least disruptive step first.

Signal loss means no cellular bars or no Wi-Fi. Cellular is the carrier's radio network. Wi-Fi is a local wireless network. First check airplane mode, a setting that switches off all radios at once. Then toggle Wi-Fi or cellular off and on. Confirm the SIM, the small chip that identifies the subscriber to the carrier, is seated and the account is active. Move to better coverage, then restart the device.

A failed app load means an app will not open, freezes, or closes right away. Force stop it, which ends the app completely. Clear its cache, the temporary files it keeps to run faster, which can become corrupted. Check free storage, then update the app and the operating system. Confirm the app supports this OS version. Reinstall only as the last app-level step.

Failed synchronization means data such as email, contacts, calendar, or photos stops matching a cloud account, an online service that holds the master copy. Common causes are no connectivity, a changed password, sync turned off for that data type, or a full cloud storage quota. A wrong date and time is another cause, because it can break the secure sign-in check.

This order works because each step is cheap and reversible and targets the most common cause first.

Worked example: a user says calendar entries made on a laptop never appear on the phone. Step 1: open a website on the phone. It loads, so connectivity is fine. Step 2: check the account in settings. It shows a sign-in error. Step 3: the user changed the password yesterday, so re-enter it. Step 4: confirm calendar sync is on and run a manual sync. The entries appear, and no data is lost.

Common mistake: jumping to a factory reset, which wipes the device back to its original state. It erases any local data that never synced and costs hours, when the real cause was often a toggle or a password. Reset only after simpler steps fail and the data is backed up.

questions.prompt:
A home-care nurse at Brightpath Health says new patient contacts added on her work tablet have not shown up on the office cloud account for three days. The technician works through it:
Step 1: Open a news website on the tablet. It loads, so connectivity is fine.
Step 2: Open the account in settings. The password was not changed, sync for contacts is switched on, and the cloud storage is only 20% used.
Step 3: ???
Step 4: Run a manual sync. The secure sign-in now succeeds and the contacts appear in the office account, with nothing lost.
Which action belongs in Step 3?
choices: Factory reset the tablet so the account is set up again from a clean state
Uninstall and reinstall the contacts app to replace any damaged files
Check the clock, which shows a date eight months off, and turn on automatic date and time
Reseat the SIM card and confirm the carrier account is still active
questions.why: With connectivity, password, the sync toggle and storage quota ruled out, a wrong date and time is the remaining common cause, because it breaks the secure sign-in check that sync depends on.

questions.prompt: A surveyor for Northline Mapping lands after a flight, and her phone shows no cellular bars and no Wi-Fi at all, even though colleagues standing beside her have full signal. What should she check first?
choices: Whether a factory reset is needed to restore the network settings
Whether airplane mode, which switches off all radios at once, is still turned on
Whether the SIM card needs to be replaced with a new one from the carrier
Whether the operating system needs an update before the radios will work
questions.why: Losing both cellular and Wi-Fi together after a flight points to airplane mode, and checking it is the cheapest, most reversible first step.

questions.prompt: At a Harbor Freight Logistics warehouse, the stock-scanning app on a handheld device closes right after opening. A technician has already force stopped it, and the problem continues. Which next step follows the least-disruptive-first approach?
choices: Factory reset the handheld so the app runs on a clean system
Turn off Wi-Fi and use only cellular data
Uninstall and reinstall the app immediately
Clear the app's cache, the temporary files it keeps to run faster, which may be corrupted
questions.why: Clearing the cache is cheap and reversible and fixes corrupted temporary files, while reinstalling is the last app-level step and a factory reset is far more disruptive.

questions.prompt: A user at Cedar Lane Dental reports that photos on his phone stopped appearing in his cloud account. Without checking anything, a technician factory resets the phone. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: Any photos stored only on the phone that never synced are erased, and the real cause, possibly a toggle or password, was never found
Nothing is lost, because a factory reset only restores settings and keeps all local files
The phone's SIM stops identifying the subscriber to the carrier until it is replaced
The photos upload faster because the reset clears the cloud storage quota
questions.why: A factory reset wipes the device back to its original state, so unsynced local data is lost, and it skips the cheap checks that usually reveal the real cause.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate is about to factory reset a user's phone because email stopped syncing. In your own words, explain how you would troubleshoot signal loss, failed app loads, and failed sync instead. Name the tradeoff of skipping straight to a reset.
lessons.modelAnswer: Start with the cheapest, most likely cause. For no signal, check airplane mode and toggle Wi-Fi or cellular. Make sure the SIM is seated and the account is active, try better coverage, then restart. For an app that will not open, force stop it, clear its cache, and check free storage. Next, update the app and the OS and confirm the app supports this OS version. Reinstall last. For sync, first confirm the phone actually has connectivity. Then check the account for a sign-in error from a changed password, confirm sync is on for that data type, check the cloud storage quota, and verify the date and time. The tradeoff with a factory reset is that it might work, but it wipes any data that never synced and takes a long time. Usually the real cause was a setting or a password, so reset only after backing up and exhausting the simpler steps.
rubricPoints: Works from simplest and most likely cause toward more disruptive fixes.
Names signal checks such as airplane mode, toggling radios, SIM or account, and restart.
Names app fixes such as force stop, clear cache, check storage, update, and reinstall last.
Names sync causes such as connectivity, changed password, sync toggle, storage quota, and date/time.
States that a factory reset risks losing unsynced data and should come only after backup and simpler steps.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine simulates a mobile device, so reasoning through exam-style symptom scenarios in the right order adds the most.

lessons.plain: A phone can be misused by software its owner never meant to trust. Three warning signs show up often. Unauthorized data access is when an app or person reads your contacts, photos, messages or accounts without real permission. Unexpected data usage is when the phone sends or receives far more internet data than your habits explain, often because something is quietly uploading in the background. Unauthorized location tracking is when something keeps reporting where you are. Think of the phone as a house with many keys: troubleshooting means finding which guest got a key they should not have, taking it back, and making sure they cannot simply walk back in.
lessons.guessPrompt: A user says their phone hit its monthly mobile data limit halfway through the month, but they have not streamed or downloaded anything new. Before touching anything else, what would you look at on the phone to find the cause?
lessons.teach:
These are three symptoms of a compromised or over-permissioned phone. A permission is a switch the mobile operating system uses to let an app reach a resource such as the camera, contacts or location. Background data is internet traffic an app uses while you are not looking at it. Location services is the feature that works out where the phone is using GPS, Wi-Fi and cell towers. Sideloading means installing an app from outside the official app store, which skips the store's screening. Rooting (Android) or jailbreaking (iOS) removes the operating system's built-in restrictions, so malware can do far more.

The approach works because the phone itself keeps records: per-app data usage, per-app permissions, and which apps recently used location. Comparing those records with what the user actually does exposes the culprit.

Worked example: a user's data cap is blown and their battery drains fast. Step 1, open data usage settings and sort by app; an unfamiliar flashlight app has used 4 GB. Step 2, check that app's permissions; it holds contacts, location and storage access, which a flashlight never needs. Step 3, check where it came from; it was sideloaded. Step 4, disconnect from networks, uninstall the app, and revoke location and background data for anything else that does not need it. Step 5, change passwords for accounts used on the phone, since data may already have been copied, and review accounts for unknown sign-ins. Step 6, apply OS updates, and if the device is rooted or the problem returns, back up personal data and factory reset (wipe the phone to its original state). Step 7, teach the user to install only from the official store and review permissions.

The common mistake is uninstalling the app and stopping there. Stolen passwords still work, other apps may hold the same permissions, and a rooted phone can be reinfected. In a workplace, a compromised phone with company email can leak business data until credentials are changed and the device is cleaned.

questions.prompt: A delivery driver at a courier company says the location arrow on his phone stays on all day, even when no map app is open. Step 1: Open the location services settings and view which apps recently used location. A 'PDF scanner' app he barely uses has checked his location dozens of times today. Step 2: MISSING. Step 3: Check where the app came from. It was installed from a link in a text message, not from the official store. Step 4: Disconnect from networks, uninstall the app, and revoke location access from any other app that does not need it. Step 5: Change passwords for accounts used on the phone, review them for unknown sign-ins, apply OS updates, and coach the driver to install only from the official store. What is Step 2?
choices: Open that app's permission list and compare what it holds, such as location, contacts and microphone, with what a PDF scanner actually needs.
Factory reset the phone right away, because any unexplained location use proves the phone is rooted.
Uninstall every app the driver installed this month so that the suspicious one is definitely removed.
Turn off location services for the whole phone and close the ticket, since the arrow will no longer appear.
questions.why: After the phone's records point to a suspect app, checking its permissions against its real purpose confirms that it is over-permissioned before you trace its source and remove it.

questions.prompt: A user says they 'sideloaded' a game onto their phone. What does that mean, and why does it matter for security?
choices: They installed the game from outside the official app store, so it skipped the store's screening.
They gave the game permission to reach the phone's storage and camera.
They removed the operating system's built-in restrictions, so any app can now do far more.
They allowed the game to use internet data while it runs in the background.
questions.why: Sideloading means installing from outside the official store, which bypasses the store's screening of apps.

questions.prompt: A sales manager at a furniture retailer has used 9 GB of mobile data in a week but says she mostly reads email. What should you do first to find the cause?
choices: Change all of her account passwords before you look at the phone.
Turn off mobile data entirely so the usage stops.
Factory reset the phone, then reinstall her apps one at a time.
Open the phone's data usage settings and sort by app to see which app used the data.
questions.why: The phone keeps per-app data usage records, so comparing them with what she actually does shows which app is responsible.

questions.prompt: At a law firm, a technician finds a malicious app on a partner's rooted Android phone that has company email on it. The technician uninstalls the app and marks the ticket resolved. Why is this not enough?
choices: Uninstalling is enough as long as the phone is restarted afterwards.
The real issue is the mobile carrier, so the technician should contact them instead.
The only remaining problem is that the app may have used extra battery.
Stolen passwords still work, other apps may hold the same permissions, and a rooted phone can be reinfected, so credentials must be changed and the phone cleaned.
questions.why: Removing the app alone leaves copied credentials usable and a rooted device open to reinfection, so company data can keep leaking until passwords are changed and the phone is updated or reset.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would troubleshoot a phone showing unexpected data usage, signs of unauthorized data access, or location tracking, and name one limit of simply uninstalling the suspicious app.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the evidence the phone already keeps. Data usage settings show which app is consuming traffic, the permissions screen shows which apps can reach contacts, storage, camera or location, and location settings show which apps recently asked for my position. Anything that uses heavy background data or holds permissions it has no reason for, especially if it was sideloaded, is the suspect. I disconnect the phone, remove that app, revoke unneeded location and background data permissions on the rest, and update the operating system. The limit of just uninstalling is that the damage may already be done: data could have been copied, so I change passwords and check accounts for strange sign-ins. If the phone is rooted or jailbroken, or the symptoms return, I back up personal data and factory reset. Finally I coach the user to install only from the official store.
rubricPoints: Uses the phone's own data usage, permission and location records to find the responsible app.
Treats excessive or unrelated permissions and sideloaded sources as red flags.
Removes the app and revokes unnecessary permissions, location access and background data.
Changes passwords and checks accounts because data may already have been taken.
Escalates to a factory reset when the device is rooted or symptoms persist.
Educates the user about trusted app sources and reviewing permissions.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine simulates a phone, so reasoning through an exam-style scenario that pairs symptoms with the right checks and remediation order builds this skill best.

lessons.plain: Documentation is the written memory of an IT team. A ticketing system is a shared to-do list where every problem or request gets its own numbered record: who reported it, what was tried, and how it ended. A knowledge base is a library of short how-to and fix articles written so the next person does not have to solve the same puzzle from scratch. Asset management is an inventory of every device and software license the organization owns, who has it, and where it is. Think of a good garage: a work-order slip for each car, a binder of repair guides, and a parts list on the wall.
lessons.guessPrompt: A user calls saying their laptop will not connect to the office printer. You fixed this exact problem for someone else last month but cannot remember how. What two things could your team have written down last month that would save you time today?
lessons.teach:
Three record-keeping tools make IT support repeatable instead of heroic.

A ticketing system is software that tracks every incident (something broken) and service request (something wanted, like a new account). Each ticket holds the user's contact details, the device, a clear description of the problem, a category, a severity or priority (how urgent and how widespread), the steps taken, any escalation (handing it to a more specialized team), and a resolution note explaining what fixed it. Good tickets are written so a stranger could pick them up mid-way.

A knowledge base (KB) is a searchable collection of articles. Each article usually covers one problem or task, states the symptoms, the cause, and numbered steps to fix it. Articles can be internal, for technicians, or external, for end users to help themselves.

Asset management is keeping an inventory of hardware and software. Each item gets an asset tag (a unique ID label), and its record lists model, serial number, location, assigned user, purchase and warranty dates, and license details. The inventory is often stored in a database tied to the ticketing system so a ticket can point to the exact device.

Worked example: a user reports the printer is unreachable. Step one, open a ticket, record the user and asset tag LT-0412. Step two, search the KB for the printer issue and find an article saying the print driver must be reinstalled after a recent update. Step three, follow it; the printer works. Step four, write the resolution in the ticket and close it. Step five, if the article was out of date, update it.

Common mistake: closing a ticket with a note like "fixed". Nobody can learn from it, recurring problems stay invisible, and the next technician repeats the whole investigation.
