In a running organization, poor records also mean lost laptops go unnoticed, warranties lapse unused, and software license counts drift out of compliance.

questions.prompt: At a small architecture firm, a designer reports that her laptop battery no longer charges past 40 percent. The technician works through it as follows. Step 1: Open a ticket recording the designer's contact details, the asset tag AF-3391, a clear description of the symptom, and a hardware category. Step 2: ??? Step 3: Find that the purchase was 14 months ago and the warranty runs for 3 years, so request a free warranty replacement instead of buying a battery. Step 4: Once the new battery works, write a resolution note in the ticket explaining that a faulty battery was replaced under warranty, then close it. Which action belongs in Step 2?
choices: Look up asset tag AF-3391 in the asset inventory to check its purchase and warranty dates
Order a replacement battery right away so the designer is not left waiting
Search the knowledge base for an article listing this laptop's purchase and warranty dates
Escalate the ticket to the network team because the laptop cannot charge
questions.why: Purchase and warranty dates are stored in the asset management record linked to the device's asset tag, so checking that record is what reveals the warranty in Step 3.

questions.prompt: A technician at a regional hospital finds a monitor labeled MN-0077 in a storage room. She needs to know its serial number, who it is assigned to, and where it should be located. Which record-keeping tool should she check?
choices: The knowledge base
An external, end-user help article
The ticket's resolution notes
The asset management inventory
questions.why: Asset management keeps an inventory record for each tagged item, including its serial number, assigned user, and location.

questions.prompt: At a logistics company, the HR manager submits a ticket asking for an email account for a new employee who starts next week. Nothing is broken. How should this ticket be classified?
choices: As an incident, because every ticket counts as an incident
As an escalation, because it involves another department
As a service request, because the user wants something new rather than reporting a fault
As a knowledge base article, because it describes a task
questions.why: An incident is something broken, while a service request is something wanted, such as a new account.

questions.prompt: At a retail chain's help desk, technicians routinely close tickets with the single word "done." What is the most likely result over time?
choices: Knowledge base articles update themselves from the ticket history
Software licenses are automatically kept in compliance
Recurring problems stay hidden and the next technician has to repeat the whole investigation
Tickets get resolved faster because there are fewer notes to read
questions.why: Without a real resolution note, nobody can learn from past fixes, repeat issues go unnoticed, and the same investigation gets done again.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a new teammate why you insist they write a full resolution note in every ticket and keep the asset inventory current, and name one cost or limit of doing this.
lessons.modelAnswer: The ticket is the only memory we have of what happened. If I write the symptom, the device's asset tag, what I tried and what actually fixed it, the next person can solve the same issue in minutes, and we can spot patterns, like ten tickets about one printer model. Good notes also turn into knowledge base articles that let users or junior techs fix things themselves. The asset inventory tells us who has which device, whether it is under warranty, and how many software licenses we use, so we do not lose hardware or fall out of license compliance. The tradeoff is time: documenting takes minutes on every ticket, and records are only useful if they are kept current. A stale knowledge base article or wrong inventory entry can mislead people, so updating it is part of the job, not an extra.
rubricPoints: States that tickets record the issue, the steps taken, and the resolution so others can continue or reuse the work.
Explains that knowledge base articles turn solved problems into reusable fixes.
Describes asset management as tracking devices and licenses, including owner, location, warranty, and tag.
Connects good records to spotting recurring problems or to license and warranty control.
Names a cost or limit, such as time spent or records going stale and misleading people.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or engine practices ticket, knowledge base, or inventory writing, and the core skill is justifying why each record matters, which explaining it back trains best.

lessons.plain: Change management is a team's agreed way of making changes to working systems without causing surprise outages. Before anyone touches a live computer, server or network, they write down what they plan to change and why, who and what it will affect, what could go wrong, and exactly how they will undo it if it fails. Then someone else reviews and approves the plan. Think of a surgeon: they do not just start cutting. They confirm the procedure, weigh the risks, and have a plan ready if things go badly. The paperwork exists to protect the systems people depend on.
lessons.guessPrompt: You are about to install an update on every computer in the accounting department the day before payroll runs. Before you start, what would you want written down and agreed, and why?
lessons.teach:
Change management is a documented, approved process for altering a production system, meaning one that people actively rely on. Three parts carry most of the weight.

Purpose and scope. The purpose is the business reason for the change, such as fixing a security hole. The scope is the boundary: which devices, users and services are affected, and what is deliberately left out. A clear scope stops a small fix from quietly growing into a large, untested one.

Risk analysis. This means estimating what could break, how likely that is, and how bad it would be, then rating the change as low, medium or high risk. Higher-risk changes usually go to a change advisory board (CAB), a group of stakeholders who approve or reject changes, and get scheduled in a maintenance window, a pre-agreed quiet time when an outage hurts least. Testing first in a sandbox, an isolated copy of the environment, lowers the risk.

Backout plan. Also called a rollback plan, this is the written, step-by-step way to return the system to its last known good state if the change fails. It must be prepared and checked before you start, because a failing change leaves no time to invent one.

Worked example. A technician needs to update the printer driver on 40 accounting PCs. Purpose: the old driver crashes during large print jobs. Scope: the 40 accounting PCs only, not the warehouse printers. Risk: medium, because payroll prints Friday. The driver is tested on two sandbox PCs first. Backout: keep the old driver installer, record its version, and allow 15 minutes per PC to reinstall it. The change is scheduled for Tuesday evening and approved. On the night, three PCs fail to print, so the technician follows the backout on those three and reopens the request.

Common mistake: treating "restore from backup" as a backout plan without confirming the backup exists, works, and fits inside the window. If you skip it, a failed change on a live system becomes an open-ended outage while users wait and the business loses work.

questions.prompt: A secondary school's technician must update the firmware on 12 wireless access points in the library building. Purpose: the current firmware has a known security flaw. Scope: the 12 library access points only. The access points in the administration building are deliberately left out. Risk: high, because students sit online exams on Thursday, so the change goes to the change advisory board (CAB). The firmware is first tested on one spare access point in a sandbox. Backout plan: ______. The change is approved and scheduled for a Saturday morning maintenance window. Which option correctly fills the missing backout step?
choices: Add the administration building's access points as well, so every device ends up on matching firmware.
Leave this step out, because the sandbox test passed and the chance of failure is now effectively zero.
Rely on restoring from a backup if anything fails, and work out the exact details on the morning itself.
Keep the current firmware file, record its version, and write timed steps to reinstall it inside the window.
questions.why: A backout plan is a written, step-by-step way back to the last known good state, prepared and checked before the change starts, and this option keeps the old firmware, records its version, and makes sure the rollback fits in the window.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic plans to replace the antivirus software on its six reception PCs because the current product is no longer receiving updates. The surgery-room PCs will keep their existing antivirus until a later project. In change-management terms, which statement describes the SCOPE of this change?
choices: The current antivirus product no longer receives updates, which leaves the reception PCs exposed.
The change carries a medium chance of blocking the clinic's booking software.
If the new antivirus fails, the old product will be reinstalled from a saved installer.
The six reception PCs are affected, and the surgery-room PCs are deliberately excluded.
questions.why: Scope is the boundary of the change: which devices, users and services are affected and what is deliberately left out. The first option is the purpose, the third is risk analysis, and the fourth is the backout plan.

questions.prompt: A law firm's technician estimates that a planned change to the email server could stop all staff from sending mail, that this is fairly likely, and that it would badly disrupt client work. The change is rated high risk. What normally happens next with a change rated this way?
choices: Risk rating is skipped for server changes, so it goes ahead the same way as a low-risk change.
It goes to a change advisory board for approval and is scheduled in a maintenance window.
Its scope is quietly widened to include other servers, which saves on a second approval later.
It is carried out right away during business hours, so that staff are on hand to report problems.
questions.why: Higher-risk changes usually need approval from a change advisory board (CAB), a group of stakeholders who approve or reject changes, and are scheduled in a maintenance window, a pre-agreed quiet time when an outage hurts least.

questions.prompt: An online shop upgrades its order database during a two-hour maintenance window. The backout plan reads only "restore from last night's backup." Nobody checked that backup beforehand. The upgrade fails, and the backup turns out to be corrupt. What was the core weakness, and what is the likely result?
choices: The backout plan was never confirmed to work or fit the window, so the failure becomes an open-ended outage.
The scope was too narrow, so the failure is limited to the database and orders continue as normal.
The risk rating was too high, so the change advisory board will now reverse the failed upgrade for them.
The window was too long, so the shop simply waits until it closes and the old system comes back on its own.
questions.why: Treating "restore from backup" as a backout plan without confirming that the backup exists, works and fits inside the window is a common mistake, and it turns a failed change on a live system into an outage with no set end while the business loses work.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says change requests are just paperwork that slows down quick fixes. Explain to them, in your own words, why purpose and scope, risk analysis, and a backout plan each matter, and name one tradeoff or limit of the process.
lessons.modelAnswer: Change management keeps a live system usable while we alter it. Writing the purpose forces us to state why the change is worth doing, and the scope fixes exactly which machines and users are touched, so a quick fix cannot grow into something nobody tested. The risk analysis asks what could break, how likely it is and how bad it would be. That rating decides whether the change needs board approval, sandbox testing, or a quiet maintenance window. The backout plan is the written way back to the last known good state, made before we start, because a failing change is the worst moment to improvise. The tradeoff is speed: the process adds review time, so a true emergency fix may go through a faster path with documentation completed afterward. A backout plan is also only as good as the backup or installer it relies on, so it has to be checked.
rubricPoints: States that purpose gives the business reason and scope limits which systems and users are affected.
Explains that risk analysis weighs likelihood and impact and drives approval, testing, and scheduling.
Defines a backout plan as a pre-written way to return to the last known good state.
Stresses that the backout plan must exist and be verified before the change begins.
Names a real tradeoff, such as slower delivery or emergency changes needing a faster path.

suggested.rationale: Rolling back a bad release under pressure shows first-hand why a scoped, risk-rated change needs a ready backout plan before it starts.

lessons.plain: A backup is a spare copy of your files kept somewhere else so you can get them back after a disk dies, a file is deleted, or ransomware scrambles everything. There are three common ways to make that copy. A full backup copies everything. An incremental backup copies only what changed since the last backup of any kind. A differential backup copies everything that changed since the last full one. Think of photocopying a notebook: copy the whole thing once, then each day copy either just today's new pages or every page written since the big copy. A backup you have never tried restoring is only a hope.
lessons.guessPrompt: You copy your whole drive on Sunday. Each weeknight after that, you save only the files that changed since the night before. The drive dies Thursday morning. Which copies would you need to rebuild Wednesday night's state, and what happens if Tuesday's copy is missing?
lessons.teach:
A full backup copies every selected file. It is the slowest to make and uses the most space, but restoring needs just that one set. An incremental backup copies only files changed since the most recent backup of any type, whether full or incremental. A differential backup copies every file changed since the last full backup. On Windows, the archive bit tracks this. The archive bit is a flag on each file that turns on when the file changes. Full and incremental backups clear the flag after copying. Differential backups leave it on, which is why each differential keeps growing until the next full.

Worked example: a full backup runs Sunday, then a nightly job runs Monday through Wednesday, and the disk fails Thursday morning. With incrementals, you restore Sunday's full, then Monday's, Tuesday's and Wednesday's incrementals, in that order. That is four sets, but each nightly job was small and fast. With differentials, you restore Sunday's full and then only Wednesday's differential, which already holds every change made Monday through Wednesday. That is two sets, but each night's job was bigger than the one before. The tradeoff: incremental means fast backups and slow restores, while differential means slower, larger backups and faster restores.

Testing a restore means actually recovering files, ideally to a separate location or machine. Then you confirm they open and are complete, and you time how long the job took. Do this on a schedule, not just once.

Common mistake: assuming backups work because the job reports success. Media can be corrupt, the wrong folders may be selected, or the encryption key may be lost. With incrementals, one damaged or missing set breaks the chain, and every change after it is lost.

In a running business, an untested backup is often found to be broken only during a real outage. That is when downtime and lost data cost the most. Keeping at least one copy offsite or offline also protects against fire and ransomware.

questions.prompt: A small accounting office runs a full backup every Saturday night and a differential backup every other night. One week, the full runs Saturday, differentials run Sunday, Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday nights, and the laptop's drive fails Thursday at noon. The technician plans the restore. Step 1: Restore Saturday's full backup, because every restore plan starts from the last full set. Step 2: ______. Step 3: Open a sample of the recovered files to confirm they are complete. What belongs in Step 2 to recover everything through Wednesday night using the fewest sets?
choices: Restore Sunday's, Monday's, Tuesday's and Wednesday's differentials, in that order
Skip the full set and restore Wednesday's differential by itself
Restore only Wednesday's differential, since it holds every change made since Saturday's full
Restore only Sunday's differential, since it was the first one after the full
questions.why: A differential copies every file changed since the last full backup, so the newest differential on top of the full already holds all changes, and only two sets are needed.

questions.prompt: On a Windows PC, the archive bit is a flag on each file that turns on when the file changes. Which backup type copies changed files but leaves that flag turned on, so its backup grows larger each night until the next full backup?
choices: Every backup type leaves the flag on
Differential
Incremental
Full
questions.why: Full and incremental backups clear the archive bit after copying, while a differential leaves it on, so each differential recopies every change since the last full.

questions.prompt: A law firm takes a full backup Saturday and incremental backups Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday nights. The server disk fails Friday. During the restore, Tuesday's incremental set turns out to be corrupt. What is the realistic outcome?
choices: Everything is recovered, because Wednesday's and Thursday's incrementals include Tuesday's changes
Thursday's incremental alone restores everything, because it is the most recent set
Only Saturday's full backup can be restored, and all incrementals are useless
Data can be restored through Monday, but changes after that point are lost because the chain is broken
questions.why: Each incremental holds only changes since the previous backup, so one damaged set breaks the chain and every change after it is lost.

questions.prompt: A community library's nightly backup job has reported success every night for six months. The IT volunteer wants real confidence that the data could be recovered. What should she do?
choices: Restore a set of files to a separate machine on a regular schedule, open them to confirm they are complete, and time how long it takes
Switch from incremental to differential backups, which never need to be tested
Run an extra full backup each week, because full backups cannot fail
Keep checking the job log each morning, since a success message confirms the copy is usable
questions.why: Testing a restore means actually recovering files, ideally elsewhere, checking they open and are complete, timing the job, and repeating on a schedule, since a success report can hide corrupt media, wrong folder choices or a lost key.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between incremental and differential backups, including what a restore needs for each, and why a restore test matters. Name the tradeoff between the two methods.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both methods start from a full backup, which copies everything. An incremental then copies only what changed since the last backup of any kind, so each nightly job is small and quick. To restore, though, you need the full plus every incremental in order, and if one is missing or corrupt, the chain breaks. A differential copies everything changed since the last full, so it grows each day. The restore is simpler: just the full plus the newest differential. The tradeoff is backup speed and storage against restore speed and simplicity. Whichever we choose, a 'completed' job doesn't prove we can recover. We should regularly restore to a test location, open the files, and time it. Otherwise we may only discover bad media, missed folders or a lost key during a real outage, when it's too late.
rubricPoints: A full backup copies everything, and a restore from it needs one set.
An incremental copies changes since the last backup of any type, and a restore needs the full plus every incremental in order.
A differential copies changes since the last full, and a restore needs the full plus the latest differential.
The tradeoff: incrementals are faster and smaller to back up but slower and more fragile to restore.
Restores must be actually tested on a schedule, because a successful job does not prove the data is recoverable.

suggested.rationale: A disaster-recovery planner would have the learner pick a backup scheme, trace which sets a restore needs after a failure, and see the cost of a broken chain or an untested backup.

lessons.plain: Safety procedures protect two things at once: the parts you are working on and the person doing the work. Your body can store a small static charge, the same kind that zaps you after crossing a carpet. Electronic chips can be damaged by a charge far too small for you to feel. Anti-static mats and wrist straps give that charge a slow, safe path away. Grounding equipment gives stray electricity a safe route into the earth instead of through a person. Safe disposal means old hardware goes to proper recycling, not the trash, because it contains harmful materials. Think of grounding as a drain that keeps electricity from pooling where it can hurt something.
lessons.guessPrompt: You walk across a carpeted office and reach into an open desktop to swap a memory stick. You feel nothing. Do you think the memory could still have been damaged, and why?
lessons.teach:
Electrostatic discharge (ESD) is the sudden flow of static electricity between two objects at different charge levels. You only feel it at roughly 3,000 volts or more, but some chips can be harmed by under 100 volts. So no spark does not mean no damage.

An ESD wrist strap is a band that touches your skin and connects by a wire, which usually contains a built-in resistor, to a ground point. Ground means a connection that leads electrical charge safely away, ultimately to the earth. The resistor drains charge slowly rather than in a jolt. An ESD mat is a mildly conductive work surface, also connected to ground, that you set parts on. Together they keep you, the mat, and the components at the same charge level, so nothing jumps between them. Anti-static bags store loose parts the same way.

Equipment grounding means mains-powered devices use a three-prong plug whose third pin connects the metal case to earth. If a live wire touches the case, current flows to ground and trips a breaker instead of passing through you. Never remove that pin or use an adapter that defeats it.

Worked example of replacing a memory module. First, shut the PC down and unplug it. Second, press the power button to drain leftover charge. Third, place the mat on the bench and clip it to a ground point. Fourth, put on the strap and clip it to the mat or to bare, unpainted chassis metal. Fifth, take the new module from its anti-static bag and handle it by the edges. Sixth, install it.

A common mistake is wearing a wrist strap while opening a power supply or other high-voltage part. The strap gives current a path through your body, and capacitors inside can hold a dangerous charge after unplugging. Power supplies are replaced whole, not opened.

Safe disposal means following local regulations and using certified e-waste recyclers, because boards and screens contain lead and other toxic metals.

In a running system, ESD damage is often latent. A part passes testing, then fails intermittently weeks later, and that is costly to trace.

questions.prompt: At a dental clinic, a technician named Priya is adding a wireless network card to a reception PC. Her reasoning, traced step by step: Step 1: Walking across the carpet has left her body carrying a static charge, possibly a few hundred volts that she cannot feel. Step 2: The new card sits on a grounded ESD mat after coming out of its anti-static bag. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: When she picks up the card by its edges, no charge jumps between her and the card, so the chips are protected. Which statement correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Her wrist strap holds the charge inside its resistor, so her body stops carrying any charge at all.
She waits until she feels a small spark, which shows her body is finally safe to touch parts.
She clips her wrist strap to the mat, so her body, the mat and the card drain to the same ground and reach the same charge level.
She touches the painted side panel once, which uses up her charge permanently for the rest of the job.
questions.why: ESD protection works by connecting the person, the mat and the part to a common ground so they share one charge level and nothing jumps between them.

questions.prompt: A technician at a print shop swaps a storage drive without a wrist strap. He felt no spark at any point, and the PC passes its tests afterward. Based on how ESD behaves, what is the most accurate conclusion?
choices: No damage happened, because passing tests right after the repair rules out any ESD harm.
Damage is still possible, because chips can be harmed well below the level a person feels, and the fault may show up as intermittent failures weeks later.
No damage happened, because ESD that harms chips always produces a visible or felt spark.
Damage is possible only if he felt a spark above about 100 volts while touching the drive.
questions.why: People feel discharges only at roughly 3,000 volts, chips can be hurt under 100 volts, and ESD damage is often latent, so passing tests does not prove the part is undamaged.

questions.prompt: An office has a metal-cased desktop with a three-prong plug, but the wall outlet only has two slots. A coworker suggests using an adapter that drops the third pin. Why is this a real safety risk?
choices: Without the third pin, a live wire touching the metal case has no path to earth, so the breaker may not trip and current could pass through a person.
It makes the PC more vulnerable to ESD during upgrades, but has no effect on shock risk.
It causes the power supply to deliver too much voltage to the motherboard.
It only matters for laptops, because desktops are grounded through their network cable.
questions.why: The third pin connects the metal case to earth so a fault sends current to ground and trips a breaker instead of passing through someone who touches the case.

questions.prompt: A school is retiring 35 old monitors and 20 desktop motherboards. Which approach matches safe disposal practice?
choices: Follow local regulations and send them to a certified e-waste recycler, because boards and screens contain lead and other toxic metals.
Store them in anti-static bags indefinitely, since that makes the toxic metals safe.
Remove the power cords and then place the rest in ordinary building waste, since the cords hold the hazardous parts.
Put them in the general trash in small batches so no single load is too heavy.
questions.why: Boards and screens contain lead and other toxic metals, so safe disposal means following local regulations and using certified e-waste recyclers.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why you bother with a wrist strap and mat for a quick part swap, how grounding protects people, and name one situation where a wrist strap is the wrong choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: Static on our bodies can damage chips at voltages far below what we can feel, so not noticing a zap proves nothing. The damage is often latent: the part works today and fails randomly later, which is expensive to diagnose. A grounded wrist strap and mat keep me and the parts at the same charge, and the resistor in the strap drains charge gently. Equipment grounding is about people. The third prong ties the metal case to earth, so a fault trips the breaker instead of running through someone. That's why we never defeat it. The limit is high voltage. I don't wear a strap when opening a power supply or anything with big capacitors, because the strap could route current through me, and we replace those units whole. Old hardware goes to a certified recycler under local rules, never the bin.
rubricPoints: ESD can damage components at voltages too low to feel, and damage may be latent.
A grounded strap and mat equalize charge and drain it safely through a resistor.
Equipment grounding via the third prong protects people by sending fault current to earth.
Never wear a wrist strap when working on high-voltage parts like power supplies.
Disposal follows local regulations through certified e-waste recyclers because hardware contains toxic materials.

suggested.rationale: No mission or engine covers physical bench safety, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios like a strap near a power supply or a three-prong adapter builds the judgment the exam tests.

lessons.plain: Some things in an IT shop are hazardous: laptop batteries can catch fire, printer toner is a fine powder you should not breathe, and cleaning chemicals can irritate skin. A Safety Data Sheet (SDS) is the manufacturer's instruction sheet for a hazardous product. It says what the dangers are, how to store it, what to do if it spills, and how to get rid of it. Disposal means following those instructions and local law instead of tossing things in the bin. Think of an SDS as the warning label and first-aid card for a product.
lessons.guessPrompt: A laptop battery has swollen so much that the case is bulging. Would you press it flat, throw it in the office bin, or do something else? Explain your reasoning.
lessons.teach:
A Safety Data Sheet (SDS) is a document the maker of a hazardous product must provide. It covers the product's hazards, safe handling and storage, the personal protective equipment (PPE, meaning gear such as gloves, goggles or a dust mask) you need, first aid, spill cleanup, and disposal guidance. IT products that have one include toner, isopropyl alcohol cleaner, thermal paste and batteries. The working rule: when you are unsure how to handle, clean up or dispose of something, read its SDS first. Then follow local regulations, which take priority because disposal law differs by city, region and country.

Batteries: lithium-ion (Li-ion) cells, the rechargeable kind in laptops and phones, can burn violently if punctured, crushed or short-circuited. A swollen cell is already damaged. Nickel-cadmium and lead-acid batteries contain toxic metals. Lead-acid batteries are the heavy ones inside a UPS (uninterruptible power supply). No battery type goes in ordinary trash. Each goes to a battery recycling point.

Toner is a fine powder of plastic and pigment. It irritates the lungs, and a cloud of it can ignite. Return empty cartridges to a manufacturer take-back program or a recycler.

Environmental controls are part of the same duty of care. Equipment needs suitable temperature, humidity and ventilation, and needs to be kept free of dust. Air that is too dry raises static discharge risk, and air that is too humid causes condensation.

Worked example, a swollen laptop battery: 1) power the laptop off and unplug it. 2) Do not press, bend or puncture the battery. 3) Check the SDS for handling advice. 4) Remove the battery if that is safe, and store it in a nonflammable container away from heat. 5) Take it to a battery recycler as local rules require, and record what you did.

Common mistake: cleaning a toner spill with a household vacuum. The particles pass straight through its filter and are blown into the room, and a spark can ignite the dust. Use a toner vacuum, which has a fine filter and anti-static design, or wipe the spill with a cloth and cold water. Warm water melts toner into a stain.

Skipping these steps causes real harm. A battery thrown in the trash can start a fire inside a garbage truck, and improper disposal can bring fines.

questions.prompt: A technician at a veterinary clinic has replaced the CPU cooler on three office PCs and has four half-used tubes of thermal paste left over. She is not sure whether they can go in the regular bin. Her process so far: Step 1, she finds the thermal paste's Safety Data Sheet (SDS) and reads its disposal guidance. Step 2 is missing. Step 3, she disposes of the tubes in the way that is allowed and writes down what she did. Which choice correctly fills Step 2?
choices: Put the tubes in ordinary trash, because thermal paste is not a battery and only batteries need special disposal
Follow the SDS alone and ignore local rules, because the maker's sheet overrides city and regional law
Check the local disposal regulations for her area, because local law takes priority over general guidance
Send the tubes to a toner cartridge take-back program, because all printer and PC supplies share that route
questions.why: The working rule is to read the SDS first and then follow local regulations, which take priority because disposal law differs by city, region and country.

questions.prompt: A new hire at a print shop must clean the rollers on a press with an isopropyl alcohol cleaner and wants to know which gloves or eye protection to wear and what to do if some splashes on skin. According to the course, which document should he consult first?
choices: The Safety Data Sheet (SDS) for the isopropyl alcohol cleaner
The local recycling center's opening hours and accepted items list
The shop's change-management log for the last maintenance visit
The printer's warranty card, which lists approved cleaning products
questions.why: The SDS is the maker-supplied document that covers a product's hazards, the protective gear needed, first aid and safe handling.

questions.prompt: During a winter heat wave of dry air, a small hosting company's equipment room reads 12% relative humidity. Based on the course, what is the main risk this creates for the equipment?
choices: Toner powder in the room melting into the air vents
Lead-acid batteries in the UPS swelling from moisture
A higher risk of static discharge damaging components
Condensation forming on circuit boards and causing shorts
questions.why: Air that is too dry raises the risk of static discharge, while air that is too humid is what causes condensation.

questions.prompt: At a city library, a toner cartridge cracks and spills powder across the floor of the print room. A staff member fills a bucket with warm soapy water and scrubs the area with a cloth. What is the most likely result?
choices: The warm water makes the toner safe to sweep up with a household vacuum
The powder dissolves completely and is safely removed from the floor
The warm water melts the toner, leaving a stain that is hard to remove
The cloth is the problem, since only a toner vacuum may ever be used on spills
questions.why: Toner is plastic and pigment powder, so warm water melts it into a stain; a cloth with cold water or a toner vacuum should be used instead.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a new teammate what an SDS is and how you would dispose of a dead laptop battery and an empty toner cartridge. Include why local regulations can override general advice, and one limit of relying on the SDS alone.
lessons.modelAnswer: An SDS, or Safety Data Sheet, is the manufacturer's sheet for a hazardous product. It lists the dangers, handling and storage, the protective gear to wear, first aid, spill cleanup and disposal. For a dead or swollen lithium-ion laptop battery, I'd power down and unplug the laptop, avoid pressing or puncturing the battery, and keep it in a nonflammable container. Then I'd take it to a battery recycler, because in the trash it can short and start a fire. An empty toner cartridge goes back to the maker's take-back program or a recycler. A spill gets a toner vacuum or a cold damp cloth, never a household vacuum. The limit is that the SDS gives general guidance, but disposal law varies by location. So local regulations come first, and the SDS alone may not tell you where to drop the item off.
rubricPoints: Defines an SDS as the manufacturer's hazard, handling, PPE, spill and disposal document.
Says lithium-ion batteries must never go in the trash and swollen ones must not be punctured or pressed.
Says batteries and toner cartridges go to recycling or take-back programs.
Says toner spills need a toner vacuum or a cold damp cloth, not a household vacuum.
Says local regulations take priority over general guidance.
Names a real consequence such as fire, health harm or fines.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine covers physical hazard handling, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios like a swollen battery or a toner spill is the best way to practise choosing the right step.

lessons.plain: This objective covers three ways a technician handles things that belong to someone else under rules. Chain of custody is a signed log of who held evidence, like a seized laptop, at every moment, so nobody can claim it was tampered with. Software licensing is the legal permission that says how many people or machines may use a program and on what terms. PII (personally identifiable information) and PHI (protected health information) are data about real people that must be kept private. Think of a museum loan: the painting has a paper trail, a contract covering how it may be shown, and guards around it.
lessons.guessPrompt: You are repairing a coworker's laptop and notice files that look like evidence of a crime. Before learning any procedure, what would you do with the laptop next, and why might it matter who touches it after you?
lessons.teach:
Chain of custody is a written, unbroken record of who held a piece of evidence (a laptop, a drive, a printout), when, and why, from discovery until it reaches the people who will use it. It works because evidence is only trusted if nobody can argue it was swapped or altered while unaccounted for.

Software licensing is the legal permission to use software on stated terms, usually set out in an end-user license agreement (EULA), the contract you accept when installing. A personal license covers one person or home use. A corporate or volume license covers many seats for a business. An open-source license makes the source code available and allows use, though it can still attach conditions. A subscription license works only while you keep paying. A perpetual license is paid once and that version is kept. Digital rights management (DRM) is technology that enforces license terms.

PII is any data that can identify a specific person, such as a name with a birth date, an ID number, or a home address. PHI is health or medical data tied to a person, and it is covered by healthcare privacy laws such as HIPAA in the US. Handling both means collecting only what is needed, limiting who can see it, encrypting it, and never copying it to personal devices or chat.

Worked example: during a repair you find files that suggest illegal activity. Step 1, stop and do not keep browsing. Step 2, report to your manager or the contact named in your company policy. Step 3, write down what you saw and when, and secure the device. Step 4, when someone takes the device, both of you sign and date the custody form. Each later handoff adds another line.

Common mistake: "just checking" the files further, or copying them to show someone. That alters the evidence and breaks the chain, so a court may refuse to accept it. The same logic applies elsewhere. Putting one personal-license copy on fifty office PCs exposes the business to audit fines, and a leaked PHI spreadsheet can trigger regulatory penalties and mandatory breach notices.

questions.prompt: A small dental practice must send last month's appointment records to an outside billing company. The records contain patient names, dates of birth, and treatment codes, so they are PHI (health data tied to a specific person). The office manager handles it like this. Step 1: she removes every column the billing company does not need, such as patients' home phone numbers and dentist notes. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: she encrypts the file before sending it. Step 4: she deletes her working copy from the shared desktop and does not save a copy to her own phone. Which action best fills Step 2?
choices: She sets the file so only the billing company's named contact can open it.
She copies the file to her personal USB stick as a backup in case sending fails.
She adds patients' home addresses so the billing company can double-check identities.
She posts the file in the office group chat so a coworker can proofread it.
questions.why: Limiting who can see PHI is one of the core handling rules, and it fits between collecting only what is needed and encrypting the file. The other choices collect extra data or copy the records to chat or a personal device.

questions.prompt: A landscape design firm pays a monthly fee for its drawing software. After the firm stops paying for two months, the software will no longer open. Which license type does this describe?
choices: Perpetual license
Subscription license
Personal license
Open-source license
questions.why: A subscription license works only while payments continue. A perpetual license is paid once, and that version keeps working.

questions.prompt: At a shipping warehouse, IT removes a hard drive from a suspect PC. The drive goes from IT to HR, and then from HR to an outside investigator. Which record keeps the chain of custody intact?
choices: A note from IT saying the drive was collected, plus a note from the investigator saying it arrived
A full copy of the drive kept by IT so the original can be passed around freely
An email from HR to the team saying the drive is now in a locked cabinet
A form logging every handoff with who gave and who received the drive, the date and time, and the reason, signed by both people
questions.why: Chain of custody needs an unbroken, written record of every holder. If any handoff is unaccounted for, someone can argue the evidence was swapped or altered.

questions.prompt: An accounting office with 12 employees buys one personal-license copy of a spreadsheet program and installs it on all 12 office PCs. What is the main risk?
choices: There is no risk because the software was paid for once.
The risk exists only if the program is open-source.
There is no risk as long as DRM does not block the extra installs.
The business breaks the license terms and could face fines in a software audit.
questions.why: A personal license covers one person or home use. A business with many seats needs a corporate or volume license, so stretching one copy across 12 PCs exposes the firm to audit fines.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a new teammate what chain of custody, software licensing, and PII/PHI handling each protect against, and name one tradeoff or limit, such as the cost of following them or what they cannot prevent.
lessons.modelAnswer: Chain of custody is a signed record of every person who held evidence, with times. If we find something illegal on a machine, we stop, report it, secure the device, and log every handoff. If there is a gap or someone pokes around in the files, the evidence can be thrown out. Licensing means we only run software the way the EULA allows. A personal copy is not a corporate license, and a subscription stops when payment stops, so installing outside those terms risks audit fines. PII identifies a person and PHI is personal health data, which privacy laws such as HIPAA cover. We keep it to the minimum we need, limit access, and encrypt it. The tradeoff is time and friction. Logging handoffs and tracking seats slows work down, and none of these rules stops a determined insider. They just make misuse detectable and show the company acted properly.
rubricPoints: Defines chain of custody as an unbroken, signed record of who held evidence and when.
Explains that gaps or tampering make evidence unusable, so the tech should stop, report, secure the device, and document.
Distinguishes license types such as personal vs corporate and subscription vs perpetual, and notes that the EULA sets the terms.
Defines PII and PHI and names handling practices: minimize, restrict access, encrypt, no personal copies.
Names a real consequence such as legal penalties, audit fines, or breach notification.
States a limit or tradeoff, such as added time or that the rules do not stop a determined insider.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or engine covers custody, licensing, or privacy handling, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios like discovering illegal content or over-installed licenses builds the judgment the exam tests.

lessons.plain: Professional communication is how a technician talks, listens and behaves so that people trust them while their problem gets fixed. It covers simple things: arriving on time, dressing appropriately, using plain words instead of jargon, listening without interrupting, staying calm when someone is upset, keeping the customer updated, and respecting their private files and space. Think of a good doctor: they ask questions, explain what they will do, don't judge you, and follow up afterwards. A technician who fixes the computer but leaves the customer confused or insulted has only done half the job.
lessons.guessPrompt: A frustrated user says, "My laptop is broken again and nobody here ever fixes anything!" Before touching the laptop, what do you think the first thing you should say or do is, and why?
lessons.teach:
Professional communication means the set of behaviours that keep a support interaction respectful, clear and productive. Exams usually group them like this. Be on time, or call ahead if you will be late. Dress for the setting. Use proper language: avoid jargon (specialist terms the listener may not know), acronyms and slang. Keep a positive attitude and project confidence, meaning you sound sure of the next step even before you know the answer. Use active listening, which means giving full attention, not interrupting, taking notes, and then restating the problem to confirm you understood it. Be culturally sensitive, for example by using the person's preferred title. Avoid distractions like personal calls, texting or social media while working. Never argue, become defensive, or dismiss a problem as minor. Set and meet expectations: give a realistic timeline, offer repair-or-replace options where they exist, and follow up afterwards. Treat customer data, desks and printouts as confidential.

Why it works: an upset person cannot give you useful facts until they feel heard. Restating and confirming the problem also stops you from solving the wrong one.

Worked example. A user snaps that printing "never works." Step 1: stay calm and don't take it personally. Step 2: listen without interrupting, and note that it started this morning on the second-floor printer. Step 3: restate it: "So since this morning, jobs to the second-floor printer don't come out?" The user adds that only PDFs fail. Step 4: explain in plain words what you will check and how long it may take. Step 5: after fixing it, confirm with the user that it works, then follow up the next day.

Common mistake: jumping straight to a fix and talking in jargon. You may fix the wrong thing, and the user cannot confirm or report back accurately. On a live system this leads to repeat tickets, missed details about scope, and lost trust, so users stop reporting problems early.

questions.prompt: At a small accounting firm, a bookkeeper calls the help desk and says, "The scanner is useless!" The technician handles it like this. Step 1: stays calm and does not take the remark personally. Step 2: listens without interrupting and writes down that, since Monday, scans sent from the fourth-floor copier to the shared folder never arrive. Step 3: ??? The bookkeeper replies, "Yes, but only scans longer than ten pages fail." Step 4: explains in plain words what will be checked and estimates about 45 minutes. Step 5: after the fix, confirms with the bookkeeper that a 12-page scan arrives, then follows up two days later. Which action belongs in Step 3?
choices: Tell the bookkeeper that scanner faults are usually minor and quick to sort out
Explain that the SMB share probably rejects the MFP's auth over the LAN
Say, "So since Monday, scans from the fourth-floor copier don't reach the shared folder?"
Start reinstalling the copier's scanning software to save the bookkeeper's time
questions.why: Restating the problem to confirm understanding is the final part of active listening, and it is what prompted the bookkeeper to add the key detail that only long scans fail.

questions.prompt: A technician at a hotel's IT desk is told by a front-desk clerk that the key-card printer keeps jamming. Which behaviour best shows active listening?
choices: Telling the clerk confidently that jams are a minor issue and not worth a ticket
Giving full attention, letting the clerk finish, taking notes, then restating the problem to confirm it
Nodding along while replying to a text, then promising to look at it later
Interrupting early to suggest the most common cause so the conversation stays short
questions.why: Active listening means full attention, no interrupting, note-taking, and restating the problem to confirm it was understood.

questions.prompt: A technician is booked for a 10:00 on-site visit to fix a point-of-sale terminal at a bakery, but traffic means arrival will be about 25 minutes late. What is the most professional action?
choices: Arrive late but work faster than usual so the total visit time stays the same
Skip the visit and reschedule by email later in the week without calling
Arrive late and apologise once on site, since the delay was outside their control
Call the bakery before 10:00, explain the delay, and give a realistic new arrival time
questions.why: Being on time includes calling ahead if you will be late, which also sets a realistic expectation for the customer.

questions.prompt: At a veterinary clinic, a technician fixes a receptionist's laptop and leaves after saying only, "Your DHCP lease expired so the NIC lost its IP; I renewed it." Next week the problem returns and the receptionist cannot describe what happened or when. What was the main communication failure?
choices: The technician used jargon and acronyms, so the receptionist could not understand or report the issue accurately
The technician should have argued that the problem was caused by the receptionist
The technician projected too much confidence about the fix
The technician did not dress formally enough for a clinic setting
questions.why: Jargon and acronyms leave the user unable to confirm the fix or report back accurately, which leads to repeat tickets and missed details.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a new teammate why active listening and setting expectations matter during a support call, and name one tradeoff or limit, such as time pressure or a customer who won't stop venting.
lessons.modelAnswer: Active listening means giving the person full attention, not interrupting, and taking notes. Then you restate the problem back, so you both agree on what is actually broken. That matters because users often describe symptoms vaguely, and confirming them stops you from fixing the wrong thing. Setting expectations means telling them what you'll do, a realistic timeline, and their options. Then you follow up, so they aren't left guessing and don't escalate out of frustration. Throughout, avoid jargon, stay calm, never argue, and keep their data confidential. The tradeoff is time. Listening fully to an upset user can feel slow when the queue is long, and some people keep venting. You still let them be heard, then politely steer back to specifics. Skipping this usually costs more time later through repeat tickets and wrong fixes.
rubricPoints: Defines active listening as full attention without interrupting, plus restating the problem to confirm it.
Explains that confirming the problem prevents fixing the wrong thing.
Describes setting expectations with a realistic timeline and options, then following up.
Mentions avoiding jargon and staying calm instead of arguing.
Names a real tradeoff such as time pressure, and how to handle it politely.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine simulates customer conversations, so explaining the techniques and their tradeoffs back in your own words is the best practice for this objective.

lessons.plain: A script is a plain text file listing commands for a computer to run in order, so a repetitive job happens the same way every time without someone typing each step. Common kinds include Windows batch files, PowerShell scripts and Python programs. Remote-access technologies let a technician reach a computer that is somewhere else, either to see its screen or to type commands on it. Together they work like a recipe card and a phone line. The recipe makes sure the job is done consistently. The phone line lets you do it from your desk instead of walking to every machine.
lessons.guessPrompt: You must connect the same shared network folder as drive S: on 50 office PCs. What would you do instead of walking to each desk, and what could go wrong if you got it slightly wrong?
lessons.teach:
A script is a text file of instructions run by an interpreter, which is a program that reads and carries out the lines one by one. Common types: batch files (.bat) run by the old Windows command prompt; PowerShell (.ps1), Microsoft's more powerful shell for managing Windows; shell scripts (.sh) for Linux and macOS; Python (.py), a general-purpose language that runs on any system; JavaScript (.js) and VBScript (.vbs). Typical uses are automating backups, restarting machines, remapping network drives, installing applications, gathering system information, and starting updates. Scripts work because a computer repeats the exact same steps every time, while a person gets tired and makes mistakes.

Worked example: you write a batch file that disconnects any old S: drive, then maps S: to the file server. Step 1: you run it on one test PC and confirm that S: opens. Step 2: you push it to all 50 PCs through a remote-management tool. Step 3: you spot-check a few machines. Fifty manual visits become one job.

Remote-access technologies: RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) shows a full Windows desktop over the network. VNC (Virtual Network Computing) shares a screen across different operating systems. SSH (Secure Shell) gives an encrypted command line, which is common on Linux. A VPN (virtual private network) is an encrypted tunnel into a private network. RMM (remote monitoring and management) tools let support teams watch and fix many machines at once. Screen-sharing and file-transfer tools fill smaller roles. Do not expose these services directly to the internet. Put them behind a VPN and use strong passwords plus multifactor authentication.

Common mistake: running an untested script, or one copied from the internet, on every machine at once. A single wrong line can change system settings everywhere, introduce malware, or loop endlessly and use up memory until systems crash. One person's error becomes a fleet-wide outage, so test on one machine first and know how to undo the change.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm keeps 12 Linux servers in its office. An admin working from home needs to run a shell script (.sh) that deletes old log files on one of those servers. Step 1: She connects to the office VPN, an encrypted tunnel into the private network, so the servers never have to be exposed directly to the internet. Step 2: ______. Step 3: At the command line she runs the .sh script and checks that disk space has been freed. Which action belongs in Step 2?
choices: Open an RDP session to the server to get a full Windows desktop
Turn off multifactor authentication on the server so the script can run without interruption
Open an SSH session to the server to get an encrypted command line
Rename the script to .bat so the old Windows command prompt can run it on the server
questions.why: SSH (Secure Shell) gives an encrypted command line and is the common way to reach Linux machines, which is exactly what she needs to run a .sh script.

questions.prompt: An IT technician at a regional hospital wants to write scripts that manage settings on hundreds of Windows computers. She wants Microsoft's more powerful shell for this, not the old command prompt. Which file type will her scripts most likely use?
choices: .sh
.ps1
.bat
.vbs
questions.why: PowerShell scripts use the .ps1 extension, and PowerShell is Microsoft's more powerful shell for managing Windows. Batch files (.bat) run in the older command prompt.

questions.prompt: A chain of 8 hardware stores wants its managers to reach their office Windows desktops from home using RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol). Which setup follows good practice for remote access?
choices: Place RDP behind a VPN and require strong passwords plus multifactor authentication
Open RDP directly to the internet on each store's router so managers can connect from anywhere
Use RDP from home without passwords, because only managers know the store's address
Replace RDP with a script copied from a forum that forwards the desktop to home PCs
questions.why: Remote-access services should not be exposed directly to the internet. They belong behind a VPN, protected by strong passwords and multifactor authentication.

questions.prompt: At a logistics company, a technician finds a cleanup script on an internet forum and pushes it to all 200 office laptops at once through the RMM (remote monitoring and management) tool. One line loops endlessly, memory fills up, and laptops across the company crash. Which practice would most likely have kept this from becoming a fleet-wide outage?
choices: Testing the script on one laptop first and knowing how to undo the change before deploying it widely
Converting the script to a different language so it runs faster
Running it twice to make sure every laptop received it
Running the script at night so fewer people notice the crashes
questions.why: Testing on a single machine first, with a way to undo the change, catches a bad line before it can hit every machine. Without that step, one person's error becomes an outage across the whole fleet.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why scripting plus remote access saves time on a fleet of PCs, and name one risk or tradeoff that comes with it.
lessons.modelAnswer: A script is a text file of commands that an interpreter runs in order. Batch files and PowerShell are for Windows, shell scripts for Linux and macOS, and Python runs almost anywhere. Instead of mapping a drive or installing an app by hand on 50 PCs, I write the steps once and they run identically everywhere. Remote-access tools deliver the work without walking to each desk: RDP or VNC to see a screen, SSH for an encrypted command line, a VPN to reach the internal network safely, and RMM tools to manage many machines at once. The tradeoff is that automation multiplies mistakes as well as effort. A bad or untrusted script can change settings, bring in malware, or exhaust memory on every machine at once. So I test on one PC first and keep a way to undo the change. Remote access also has to sit behind a VPN with MFA, not open to the internet.
rubricPoints: Defines a script as a file of commands run in order by an interpreter.
Names at least two script types and matches them to their platforms.
Gives a concrete use case such as mapping drives, installing software, or backups.
Names remote-access tools such as RDP, SSH, VPN or RMM and what each does.
States a risk: untested or untrusted scripts can cause fleet-wide damage, malware or crashes.
Mentions a safeguard: test on one machine, secure remote access with VPN and MFA.

suggested.rationale: Writing a first script that automates a routine system-information report gives hands-on practice with the core scripting use case, though the remote-access half of this objective still has to be learned from the reading.

scenarios.title: First Week on the Help Desk at Larkfield Veterinary Group
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined the small IT team at Larkfield Veterinary Group, a fictional chain of three animal clinics. Your lead hands you four tickets from the front-desk office and asks you to use the right built-in tool for each one rather than clicking around hoping to find the setting.

Ticket A: The reception PC runs Windows 11 and has become very slow. A process (a program that is currently running in memory) seems to be using almost all of the CPU (the processor, the chip that carries out instructions). Staff cannot close it normally.

Ticket B: A technician fitted a brand-new second hard drive in the records PC so it can hold X-ray images. Windows starts fine, but the new drive does not appear in File Explorer. A brand-new drive has no partition (a section of the disk that the operating system treats as a separate unit) and no volume (a partition that has been formatted with a file system and given a drive letter). A file system is the method an OS uses to organise and track files on a disk; Windows normally uses NTFS.

Ticket C: The clinic is moving to a domain. A domain is a centrally managed group of computers and user accounts controlled by a server called a domain controller, so one administrator can manage logins and policies for everyone. The alternative, a workgroup, is a set of computers that each manage their own accounts. One new laptop was bought with Windows 11 Home edition (an edition is a version of Windows sold with a particular set of features), and the option to join the domain is missing.

Ticket D: The clinic's appointment system runs on a small Linux server. Linux is a free, open-source operating system often used on servers. Users report that saving appointments fails, and the vendor suspects the server's disk is full. You have a terminal (a text window where you type commands) open on the server.

Your tasks:
1. For Ticket A, name the Windows tool you would use, one quick way to open it, and the steps to find and stop the process using the CPU.
2. For Ticket B, name the Windows tool you would use and list, in order, the steps to make the new drive usable with a drive letter.
3. For Ticket C, explain why the laptop cannot join the domain and what change fixes it, and say whether that fix needs a clean install.
4. For Ticket D, give the Linux command that shows how much space is used and free on each mounted file system in human-readable sizes, and say what you would look for in the output.
modelAnswer: Use Task Manager, the built-in Windows tool that shows running processes and how much CPU, memory, disk and network each one uses. Open it quickly with Ctrl+Shift+Esc (or right-click the Start button and choose Task Manager, or Ctrl+Alt+Delete then Task Manager). On the Processes tab, select the CPU column heading to sort so the heaviest user is at the top, identify the process using near 100 percent CPU, select it, and choose End task. Common mistake: ending a core Windows process you do not recognise, which can crash or restart the system, so check what the process is first. If the problem keeps coming back, investigate the program that starts it rather than ending it every time.

Use Disk Management, the built-in Windows tool for managing disks, partitions and volumes (open it by right-clicking Start and choosing Disk Management, or by running diskmgmt.msc). Steps: 1) When Disk Management opens it should prompt you to initialize the new disk; if not, right-click the disk and choose Initialize Disk. Pick a partition style, normally GPT (GUID Partition Table, the modern style that supports large disks; MBR is the older style). 2) Right-click the unallocated space and choose New Simple Volume. 3) Set the size (usually all available space). 4) Assign a drive letter, for example E:. 5) Format it with the NTFS file system and give it a label such as Xrays. 6) Finish; the drive now appears in File Explorer. Common mistake: formatting or deleting the wrong disk, which erases its data, so confirm the disk by its size and the fact that it shows as unallocated before acting.

Windows Home edition cannot join a domain; that feature is only in business-level editions such as Windows 11 Pro, Enterprise or Education. The fix is to upgrade the laptop from Home to Pro, typically by entering a Pro product key or buying the upgrade in Settings > System > Activation. This is an in-place upgrade (the edition changes while the user's files, settings and apps are kept), so a clean install (wiping the disk and installing fresh) is not required. After the upgrade, join the domain through Settings or System Properties using a domain account allowed to add computers, then restart. Back up the user's data first as a sensible precaution.

Run df -h. The df command reports disk space for each mounted file system, and the -h option shows sizes in human-readable units such as G for gigabytes instead of raw block counts. In the output, look at the Use% and Avail columns, especially for the file system mounted at / (the root) or wherever the application stores its data. A value at or near 100 percent with little or nothing available confirms the disk is full, which explains why saves fail. (du -sh on a folder can then help find which directories are using the space.) Common mistake: deleting files at random to free space, which can break the application; find the large files first and remove only what is safe, such as old logs.

scenarios.title: Locking Down a Small Dental Office After a Rough Week
scenarios.scenario:
You have just started as the only IT support technician at Harlow & Pine Dental, a fictional eight-person dental practice. The office has a front desk, two treatment rooms, a back staff door that opens onto the car park, and one wireless network. In one week, the office manager reports four problems.

First, a stranger walked in through the back staff door by following closely behind a hygienist. Following someone through a door they unlocked, without using your own access, is called tailgating. On the same day, the front-desk laptop, which stores patient appointment data, nearly walked out with a visitor. It was sitting loose on the counter.

Second, the Wi-Fi uses WPA2-Personal. WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) is a standard that encrypts wireless traffic, meaning it scrambles the data so outsiders cannot read it. The Personal mode means everyone shares one password, called a pre-shared key. A dental assistant who left the company last month on bad terms still knows that password, and staff have spotted her car in the car park.

Third, the receptionist downloaded a free 'invoice viewer' from an email link. Since then the PC shows pop-ups and runs slowly, and the security software flags a trojan. A trojan is malicious software, or malware, that pretends to be a useful program so the user installs it willingly. The receptionist's Windows account is a local administrator, which means it can install software and change system settings without restriction.

Fourth, the office manager asks what would happen to the patient data if the front-desk laptop were stolen anyway. The laptop runs Windows and has a TPM. A TPM (Trusted Platform Module) is a small security chip on the motherboard that can safely store encryption keys.

Your tasks:
1. Recommend one physical control for the back staff door and one for the front-desk laptop, and explain what each control stops.
2. Explain why the former employee is still a risk to the Wi-Fi network, and describe a better wireless setup using WPA3 or 802.1X with a RADIUS server.
3. Describe the steps to deal with the infected receptionist PC, in order, and name two settings changes that make a repeat less likely.
4. Recommend the Windows feature that protects the laptop's data if it is stolen, explain how it works in simple terms, and name one thing you must do so the office does not lock itself out.
subParts: Physical controls for door and laptop
Protecting data on a stolen laptop
modelAnswer: For the back staff door, install a badge reader. This is an electronic lock that only opens when an authorised staff card is held against it, and it records who entered and when. A stronger option is a mantrap: a small space between two doors where the second door will not open until the first one has closed, so only one person passes through at a time. A mantrap directly stops tailgating. A badge reader alone stops strangers from opening the door themselves, but it must be paired with staff training to never hold the door for someone they do not know. For the front-desk laptop, use a cable lock. This is a steel cable that loops around a fixed object, such as the desk, and plugs into the laptop's lock slot, so the laptop cannot be quickly picked up and carried off. A common mistake is relying on a password alone. A password does nothing to stop someone from physically carrying the device away.

The risk exists because WPA2-Personal uses one shared password for everyone. Removing one person's access means changing the password and re-entering it on every device. Until that happens, the former employee can still join the network from the car park and reach the office computers. As an immediate step, change the Wi-Fi password and disable any accounts she still has. The better long-term setup is per-user authentication, using WPA2-Enterprise or WPA3-Enterprise. In this setup, 802.1X is the standard that makes each user or device prove its identity before it is allowed onto the network. A RADIUS server (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) is the central server that checks each person's own username and password, or certificate, and says yes or no. When someone leaves, you disable only their account on the RADIUS server, and nobody else is affected. If an enterprise setup is too complex for the office, at minimum move to WPA3-Personal, which uses stronger encryption and resists password-guessing attacks better than WPA2. Even then, you must still change the shared password whenever staff leave.

Steps, in order. (a) Confirm the symptoms match malware, which they do: pop-ups, slowness, and a security alert. (b) Quarantine the PC by unplugging the network cable or disabling Wi-Fi, so the trojan cannot spread or send data out. (c) Disable System Restore, so infected restore points are not kept and used to bring the malware back. (d) Update Microsoft Defender's malware definitions and run a full scan to remove the threat. If the malware resists removal or hides itself, as a rootkit does, run a Microsoft Defender Offline scan, which checks the system before Windows fully starts. (e) Schedule regular scans and keep updates turned on. (f) Re-enable System Restore and create a new, clean restore point. (g) Teach the receptionist to spot phishing, which means fake emails designed to trick people into clicking links or downloading files. Two prevention changes: first, apply least privilege by changing the receptionist to a standard user account, so she cannot install software without an administrator approving it. Second, keep User Account Control (UAC) turned on. UAC is the Windows prompt that asks for approval or an administrator password before changes are made to the system. Together these mean a fake installer cannot quietly install itself.

Use BitLocker, the full-disk encryption feature built into Windows. Full-disk encryption scrambles everything stored on the drive. The key needed to unscramble it is held by the TPM and released only when that laptop starts up normally, optionally after the user enters a PIN. If a thief removes the drive and connects it to another computer, they see only unreadable data, so the patient records stay protected. To avoid locking the office out, back up the BitLocker recovery key before relying on it. This is a long number that unlocks the drive if the TPM or the startup check fails, for example after a hardware change. Store it somewhere safe and separate from the laptop, such as the company's Microsoft account or a printed copy in a locked safe. A common mistake is enabling BitLocker without saving the recovery key. If the drive later asks for that key, the data on it can be permanently lost.

scenarios.title: Fake Virus Warnings at Brightwater Bakery Supply
scenarios.scenario:
You are a new desktop support technician at Brightwater Bakery Supply, a fictional wholesale baking-goods company. Priya, an order clerk, calls the help desk about her Windows 11 Home laptop, which is connected to the office network.

She reports three things. First, when she types the company's supplier portal address into her web browser, she lands on an unfamiliar shopping site instead. This is called browser redirection: something has changed the browser or system settings so that requests are sent to a page the user did not ask for. Second, small advertising windows keep opening on their own, even when no browser is open. These are unwanted pop-ups, meaning windows that appear without the user requesting them. Third, a program she never installed, called "PC Shield Ultra", shows a red alert saying 47 viruses were found and asks her to pay $59.99 to remove them. This is rogue antivirus: fake security software that invents scary warnings to scare the user into paying or installing more harmful software. Priya clicked "Scan Now" in that program yesterday but did not pay.

Your senior colleague reminds you of a few terms. Malware is any software built to harm a computer or its user, or to trick them. To quarantine a system means to isolate it, for example by unplugging the network cable and turning off Wi-Fi, so the malware cannot spread to other computers or send data out. System Restore is a Windows feature that saves snapshots of system files and settings, called restore points, so the computer can be rolled back to an earlier state. Malware can hide inside those restore points. To remediate means to actually remove the infection, using anti-malware software (a legitimate security scanner) after updating its definitions, which are the up-to-date list of known threats it searches for. Remediation is often done in Safe Mode, a Windows startup mode that loads only the basic drivers and services, so many malware programs cannot start and defend themselves.

Another new technician suggests simply finding the "PC Shield Ultra" folder, deleting it, and handing the laptop back. Your colleague says that skips most of the correct procedure.

1. Explain what Priya's three symptoms together tell you about the laptop, and why you should treat them as a malware problem rather than three separate unrelated faults.
2. Put these steps into the correct best-practice order: (a) remediate the infection with updated anti-malware, using Safe Mode if needed; (b) educate the user; (c) quarantine the laptop; (d) investigate and confirm the malware symptoms; (e) disable System Restore; (f) re-enable System Restore and create a fresh restore point; (g) schedule regular scans and apply updates.
3. Explain why System Restore is disabled before remediation and why it is re-enabled with a new restore point afterward, including what could go wrong on Priya's laptop if you skipped either part.
4. Explain why only deleting the "PC Shield Ultra" folder is not enough, and describe two things you would tell Priya during the user-education step.
subParts: Reason for disabling and re-enabling System Restore
Why deleting one folder fails, and user education
modelAnswer: Browser redirection, unwanted pop-ups appearing even with no browser open, and a rogue antivirus program she never installed are all classic signs of a malware infection. Together they point to unwanted software that has changed browser or system settings, runs on its own in the background, and is trying to trick Priya into paying. Because the symptoms appeared together and none came from software she chose to install, the likely single cause is malware, quite possibly several pieces installed together. That is why the correct malware-removal procedure applies instead of fixing each symptom on its own. Clicking "Scan Now" in the fake program may have let even more harmful software in, so the laptop should be treated as compromised.

The correct order is d, c, e, a, g, f, b. First investigate and confirm the symptoms (d). Then quarantine the laptop by disconnecting it from the network so the malware cannot spread or send data out (c). Next disable System Restore (e). Then remediate with anti-malware whose definitions have been updated, working in Safe Mode if the malware resists (a). After cleaning, schedule regular scans and apply updates (g). Then re-enable System Restore and create a new restore point (f). Finally educate the user (b). A key point is that quarantine comes before any cleanup, so the infection cannot reach other Brightwater computers while you work.

System Restore is disabled first because malware can be saved inside existing restore points. If those points remain, rolling back later, by you or by Windows, could bring the infection straight back even after a successful scan. Disabling the feature clears those possibly infected snapshots. After the system is clean, System Restore is turned back on and a fresh restore point is made, so there is a known-good snapshot to recover from if a future problem occurs. If you skip disabling it, Priya's laptop could be reinfected from an old restore point. If you skip re-enabling it, the laptop has no recovery safety net, so a later bad update or driver could leave it with no easy way to roll back.

Deleting one folder only removes the most visible piece. The redirection and pop-ups show that other components, such as changed browser settings or hidden background programs, are probably present too. Malware often reinstalls itself from parts you did not find. Deleting the folder also skips quarantine (other PCs stay at risk), skips clearing infected restore points, skips a full scan with updated definitions, and skips user education, so the same thing is likely to happen again. In the education step, tell Priya that real security software does not demand payment through a pop-up, so she should never click buttons in unexpected security warnings and should call the help desk instead. Also tell her to install software only from approved sources, keep the system updated, and report odd behavior such as redirected websites right away.

scenarios.title: The Accounts Workstation SSD Swap at Harbor Lane Supply
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined the small IT team at Harbor Lane Supply, a fictional company that distributes baking ingredients to cafes. The accounts workstation, the one desktop PC that holds the company's invoicing data, is running out of disk space. Your lead asks you to replace its old 256 GB SSD (solid-state drive, a storage drive with no moving parts) with a new 1 TB SSD on Thursday morning. You will copy the existing system onto the new drive with a cloning tool, which is software that makes an exact copy of one drive onto another.

Your lead reminds you of some terms.
