Change management is the agreed process for planning, approving, and recording any change to a live system, meaning one people rely on for daily work, so changes do not cause surprise outages. A change request should state the purpose (why the change is needed), the scope (exactly what will be touched and what will not), a risk analysis (what could go wrong, how likely it is, and how bad it would be), and a backout plan (the exact steps to undo the change and return to the last working state if it fails).

Backups are copies of data kept so it can be recovered. A full backup copies everything selected. An incremental backup copies only what changed since the last backup of any type, so a restore needs the last full backup plus every incremental after it, applied in order. A differential backup copies everything changed since the last full backup, so a restore needs only the last full backup plus the newest differential. A restore test means actually recovering data from a backup to prove the backup works. Harbor Lane ran a full backup of this PC on Sunday night and incremental backups on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday nights.

ESD (electrostatic discharge) is the sudden jump of static electricity from your body to a component. It can damage chips even when you feel no spark. An ESD strap is a wrist band connected by a wire to a ground point, and an ESD mat is a work surface also connected to ground. Both let static drain away slowly and safely. Grounding means giving electricity a safe path to the earth.

For documentation, Harbor Lane uses a ticketing system (software that records each request or problem, who is handling it, and what was done), asset management records (a list of the company's hardware and software, with details like serial numbers, location, and who uses each item), and knowledge base articles (written how-to guides the team can reuse later).

Your tasks:
1. Write the four key parts of the change request for this SSD swap: purpose, scope, risk analysis, and backout plan.
2. If the swap fails on Thursday morning and the invoicing data must be restored from backup, list which backup sets you need and in what order. Then explain why a restore test should happen before the change, not after.
3. Describe the safety steps you take while physically opening the PC and swapping the drive, and say what could happen to the running system if you skip them.
4. After a successful swap, name what you update in the ticketing system, the asset management records, and the knowledge base, and give one real risk of skipping this step.
subParts: Backup restore order and restore testing
modelAnswer: Purpose: the accounts workstation is nearly out of disk space, which threatens invoicing, so the 256 GB SSD is being replaced with a 1 TB SSD. Scope: only the accounts workstation's internal drive is touched. The operating system and data are cloned unchanged, with no software upgrades and no other PCs involved. Risk analysis: the clone could fail or be incomplete, the new drive could be faulty, the PC might not boot from the new drive, or static could damage parts. The likelihood is low to moderate, but the impact is high because this PC holds the invoicing data, so the work is scheduled outside busy invoicing hours and only after a verified backup. Backout plan: keep the original 256 GB SSD unchanged and labelled. If the new drive fails to boot or data is missing, power down, reinstall the original SSD, boot, and confirm invoicing works. If the original drive is also unusable, restore from backup. A strong answer includes all four parts and makes the backout steps concrete, not just 'undo the change'.

Restore order: first the Sunday full backup, then the Monday incremental, then Tuesday, then Wednesday, applied in that order. Each incremental holds only the changes since the backup before it, so skipping one or applying them out of order leaves data missing or inconsistent. A restore test should happen before the change because a backup that has never been restored is not proven to work. The files could be corrupt, incomplete, or the wrong data. If you only discover this after the swap has failed, there is no safe way back and invoicing data could be lost permanently. Testing first turns the backout plan from a hope into a known safety net.

Shut the PC down fully and unplug the power cable. Place the PC and the new SSD on an ESD mat, wear an ESD strap clipped to a proper ground point, and keep the new drive in its anti-static bag until you install it. Handle drives by the edges and avoid touching the contacts or chips. Static can be too weak to feel but still strong enough to damage the new SSD or the motherboard. Damage may cause immediate failure, or it may cause hidden weakness that shows up later as random crashes or data corruption on the invoicing PC, long after the change seems to have worked. The old SSD holds company data, so it must be kept secure and later disposed of safely, not thrown in the bin.

Ticketing system: record what was done, when, by whom, the result, and any problems, then close the ticket and link it to the approved change request. Asset management: update the workstation's record with the new 1 TB SSD (model and serial number) and record the old drive's status, such as kept as a backout spare, stored securely, or awaiting secure disposal. Knowledge base: write or update an article with the cloning and swap steps and any gotchas found, so the next person can repeat the job reliably. Example risk: if the asset record still lists the old drive, the team may later lose track of a drive containing invoicing data, or troubleshoot and order parts for the wrong hardware. Accept any one realistic consequence.
